prose: Overview

This is the first challenge in the module, and it is different from every one that follows: you will not build anything today. Before you build a single mechanism, you need a way of thinking about problems — a process you can run every time, whether the problem is sorting poms or lifting a load or moving something across a field.

You will learn that process here and watch it applied to a real engineering problem that took decades to solve. Every challenge sheet after this one is written in its language — a Problem, a Need, Constraints, and sometimes an Added Value — so an hour spent here pays off twenty-six times.
Core Insight
Engineers do not start by building. They start by defining — what the problem actually is, what the solution must do, and what limits it has to stay inside.
A design that solves the wrong problem beautifully is still a failure.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Explain what makes engineering different from science.
Name and use the five steps of the engineering design process , and recognize the same work in an eight-step version.
Tell the difference between a need and a constraint, and write both clearly.
Explain what a success rate is, and why engineers measure with a count instead of an impression.
Portions of this module are adapted from materials freely distributed by the Royal Academy of Engineering.
Phase 1 — What Is Engineering?

Engineering is the branch of STEM concerned with the design, building, and use of engines, machines, and structures. It is a wide field, so it is usually broken into disciplines — mechanical, electrical, civil, chemical, software, and many more.
How Engineering Differs from Science
Science asks what is true. Engineering asks what can be made. The dividing line is design.
From the Royal Academy of Engineering

Design is the essential creative process of engineering, which distinguishes it from science, and which calls for imagination, creativity, the knowledge and application of technical and scientific skills, and skillful use of materials.

Read that again and notice what is in the list. Imagination and creativity come first — before technical skill. That is not decoration. An engineer who knows every formula but cannot picture a new arrangement of parts will not produce a new machine.
In your own words: what is the difference between a scientist studying how gears transmit force and an engineer using gears to build a claw?
Phase 2 — The Engineering Design Process
There is more than one way to describe how engineering gets done. The version below has five steps. You will use it on every challenge in this module, so learn it here.
A Second Way to Describe the Same Work
Engineers do not all use the same map. Here is an eight-step version of the same territory. Read it next to the five-step flowchart above.
Define the Problem
Do Background Research
Specify Requirements
Brainstorm Solutions
Choose the Best Solution
Do Development Work
Build a Prototype
Test and Redesign

Notice that nothing new appears — the eight steps slice the same loaf thinner. “Specify Requirements” is needs and constraints. “Test and Redesign” is the loop back at the bottom of the flowchart. The number of steps is a choice; the discipline of defining before building is not.
Match them up: which of the eight steps fold into step 1 of the five-step process, and which fold into step 5? Where does brainstorming fit?
Needs and Constraints Are Not the Same Thing
Students mix these up constantly, so be precise. A need is what the design must accomplish. A constraint is a limit the design must stay inside while accomplishing it.
Need
What the thing has to do . “Lift four poms into a container.”
Constraint
A limit it has to obey . “Using no more than two motors.”
Constraints come in three shapes:
Minimums — the design must reach at least this much. At least 3 inches wide.
Maximums — the design must not exceed this. No more than two motors.
Approximations — close enough counts. Roughly the size of a soda can.
Added Value
Some challenges also list an added value : something beyond the minimum that makes the design genuinely better. Meeting the need gets you a working machine. Added value gets you a good one.
Write one need and one constraint for a completely different problem — a backpack, a bike rack, a lunch tray, anything. Make sure the need says what it does and the constraint says what limits it.
Phase 3 — A Worked Example: The Turning Car
Here is the process run on a real problem. It is worth studying because the problem was not obvious — it stayed hidden inside a bigger machine for years before anyone named it properly.
Step 1 — Define the Problem

When a car turns a corner, the two rear wheels do not travel the same distance. The wheel on the inside of the turn follows a tighter circle than the wheel on the outside. The outside wheel has farther to go, in the same amount of time.

In cars built in the 1920s, the rear wheels were fixed to a single solid axle. The motor drove both wheels at exactly the same speed. But the road demanded different speeds. Something had to give — and what gave was the inside tire, which slipped and scrubbed across the pavement on every turn, wearing out early.
Step 2 — Determine the Need
Find a way to let the two wheels spin at different rates while the car turns, while still letting the motor power both of them.
Step 3 — Determine the Constraints
The mechanism must fit inside the chassis of the car.
It must be cheap enough to justify putting in every car built.
It must not interfere with the other jobs the rear axle already does.
Step 4 — Break It Down
Engineers did not solve this in one leap. They broke it into stages:
Create a device that lets the wheels turn independently of each other.
Modify that system so it responds automatically instead of being set by hand.
Convert it into a sealed, self-contained unit that fits the space and wastes little motor power.
Step 5 — Does It Meet the Need?
Watch what they arrived at. This mechanism is in nearly every car on the road today.
The automotive differential.
Which of the three constraints do you think was hardest to satisfy, and why?
Step 4 broke one huge problem into three smaller ones. Why does breaking a problem down make it easier to solve — and not just easier to describe?
Phase 4 — How Engineers Measure Success
Step 5 of the process asks whether the result meets the needs. That question sounds like an opinion. Engineers refuse to let it be one.
A Count, Not an Impression
A success rate is not a feeling about how well something went. Run a device 10 times and count how many times it fully worked. That count is the percentage — 9 successes out of 10 runs is 90%.

Many challenges in this module set a bar of greater than 90%. To beat it, you need 10 out of 10, or 19 out of 20. That bar is demanding on purpose: a machine that works 8 times out of 10 will fail you at a competition.

This is also why iteration is step 5’s loop back and not a punishment. The first version is expected to fail some runs. The count tells you honestly how often, and the failed runs tell you what to change.
A teammate says, “It basically works — it sorted the poms both times we tried it.” Using what you just read, explain what is wrong with that sentence, and what you would ask the teammate to do next.
Phase 5 — Connect: Where This Shows Up in Botball
Transfer

Every challenge sheet in this module is written in the language you just learned: a Problem, a Need, Constraints, and sometimes an Added Value. So is Botball itself. A game rulebook is one long list of needs and constraints — what scores, what is allowed, what size box the robot must start inside.

The working end of every machine you will build here — the claw, the scoop, the arm — is called an effector . Every mechanism in Challenges 3 through 28 exists to make some effector do its job, and every one of those sheets will hand you a need and a set of constraints first. Now you know why.
Where the Design Projects Went

The original version of this material ends with open design projects — a pom sorter and a 17-inch lift — where you run the whole process on a problem with no instructions. Those projects are still here, waiting at the end of the module as Design Project A and Design Project B . Come back to them once you own a few mechanisms; they will go far better then.
Pick any scoring task from this year’s Botball game. Write it as one need and two constraints, and mark each constraint as a minimum, a maximum, or an approximation.

Botball could simply say “build the best robot you can.” Instead it sets strict constraints — a starting size box, banned materials, a time limit. What do constraints like these do for the teams, not just to them?
Phase 6 — Individual Reflection
Complete this section on your own.
1. List the five steps of the engineering design process from memory. Then say which one you think teams skip most often — and what goes wrong when they do.
2. Explain the difference between a need and a constraint, using one example of each that you wrote today.
3. The turning-car problem hid inside a bigger machine for years before anyone defined it clearly. Why does a fuzzy problem statement make a problem so much harder to solve?
4. Complete this in 2–3 sentences: “A design that solves the wrong problem beautifully is still a failure. This means that before I build anything, I should...”
Extension Challenges
Finished early? Try one or more of these. Still no parts required.
Extension A — Spec an Everyday Object
Pick a machine you used today — a stapler, a bike, a vending machine, a door closer.
Reverse-engineer its paperwork: write the Problem it solves, its Need, three Constraints its designers must have faced, and one Added Value it delivers.
Mark each constraint as a minimum, a maximum, or an approximation.
Extension B — Constraint Hunt in the Rulebook
Open this year’s Botball game rules.
Find one minimum constraint, one maximum constraint, and one approximation. Quote or paraphrase each.
Which single constraint do you think will shape robot designs the most this season, and why?
Extension C — Run the Process on Paper
Take the turning-car problem and pretend the differential was never invented.
Brainstorm two other ways to let two wheels turn at different speeds. Wild ideas welcome — brainstorming forbids criticizing.
For each idea, name the constraint from Step 3 it would struggle with most.
Extension D — Write the Challenge
Invent a new design problem for a classmate. Write it as a Problem, a Need, and three Constraints.
Trade with someone and critique each other’s: is the need testable? Is each constraint classified correctly? Could you tell, with a count, whether a design succeeded?
What was hard about writing constraints that were demanding but still possible?

prose: Overview

Challenge 1 gave you the process. This sheet gives you the component that nearly every mechanism in this module is built from: the gear. Like Challenge 1, there is nothing to build today — this is knowledge you will spend from Challenge 3 onward.

Gears look like magic the first time you watch a small motor lift something heavy through them. They are not magic. Everything a gear pair does — reversing direction, trading speed for strength, holding a load — comes down to counting teeth. By the end of this sheet you will be able to do that counting yourself.
Core Insight
Gears aren’t magic. For everything we gain, we give something else up.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Explain why meshed gears must turn in opposite directions, and how an idler gear changes that.
Predict how far one gear turns when another turns, by counting teeth.
Calculate a gear ratio , and say which way it trades speed against torque .
Multiply ratios through compound gearing — and name the price you pay for the gain.
Phase 1 — Why Gears? A Claw With a Problem

Here is where the need comes from. A simple demo-bot claw has one fixed side and one moving side. It works — but as the moving jaw closes, it shoves the object sideways against the fixed jaw. For some tasks that is fine. For many, it is not.

Suppose the task needs both sides of the claw to move in and out, in coordination with each other — a pincer . Presumably we want each arm to mirror its counterpart exactly. But how is this accomplished?
The Answer, and the Whole Point of This Sheet

One way to make both arms move in predictable patterns compared to one another is with gears at the base of each arm. Put a gear on each arm, mesh the two gears together, and turning one arm must turn the other. From that moment on, the arms cannot disagree.
If the gear on the left turns clockwise, what happens to its arm?
What direction does this force the other arm to move? Does this meet the need — both jaws closing together?
Phase 2 — Teeth and the Mesh

Gears, or sprockets, have a set number of teeth. For a pair of gears to work together, their teeth must share a mesh location — a spot where the teeth of one interlock with the teeth of the other. Once two gears mesh, neither can turn without turning the other.
Here is the model that makes everything on this sheet countable. Every tooth that passes through the mesh is one click . Both gears feel every click — the mesh guarantees it.

So turn the 10-tooth gear one full rotation: 10 clicks pass through the mesh. The 8-tooth gear receives those same 10 clicks — but it only needs 8 for a full turn. It turns a full rotation and then some . The smaller gear always spins farther than the larger one it meshes with.
If Your Kit Is Nearby (Optional)

Everything on this sheet can be answered without parts. But if your kit is in reach, mesh a small gear with a large one, mark one tooth on each with a bit of tape, and turn the small gear exactly one rotation. Watch what the large one does. The click model is not a metaphor — you can hear it.
A 16-tooth gear makes one full rotation. How many clicks pass through the mesh? If it is meshed with an 8-tooth gear, how many rotations does the 8-tooth gear make from those clicks?
Phase 3 — Direction: The Rule and the Trick
Look back at the pincer diagram in Phase 1 and notice what the mesh did to direction.
The Direction Rule
Two meshed gears always turn in opposite directions. Always. The teeth leave them no choice.
For the pincer that rule was exactly what we wanted — opposite rotations close the two jaws together. But suppose a task needs two arms to move in the same direction. Are gears useless then?

No — place a third gear between them. Direction now reverses twice: the left gear reverses the middle one, and the middle one reverses the right one. The two outer gears end up turning the same way. A gear used like this — in the middle, only to manage direction — is called an idler gear . It changes direction without changing the ratio between the outer gears.
The three gears can be drawn staggered or sit in a straight line — the geometry does not change the rule.

Four gears sit in a straight line, all meshed neighbor-to-neighbor. The leftmost turns clockwise. Work along the line: what direction does each of the other three turn? State the pattern for any number of gears.
Phase 4 — Gear Ratio: Trading Speed for Strength

Now use the click model on gears of different sizes — this is where gears earn their keep. Mesh an 8-tooth gear with a 16-tooth gear and turn the 8-tooth gear one full rotation clockwise. Eight clicks pass through the mesh. The 16-tooth gear needs sixteen clicks for a full turn, so it turns exactly half a rotation — counterclockwise, by the direction rule.
That pair has a gear ratio of 16:8, which reduces to 2:1 — the drive gear (the one the motor turns) must turn twice for every one turn of the driven gear (the one being turned).
Torque
Just as a linear force is a push or a pull, a torque can be thought of as a twist to an object.
Using meshed gears with different tooth counts gives us an advantage, and it runs both ways:
Turn the smaller gear in the pair, and the larger one turns slower but with more torque — a stronger twist.
Turn the larger gear , and the smaller one turns faster but with less torque — more speed.
If you want a very large amount of torque, turn a gear with a low number of teeth against a gear with a high number of teeth. An 8-tooth gear driving a 30-tooth gear gives a 30:8 ratio — 3.75:1 .

A 12-tooth drive gear meshes with a 36-tooth driven gear. Write the ratio in both forms (teeth and reduced). If the drive gear turns 6 full rotations clockwise, how many rotations does the driven gear make, and in which direction?

You are choosing gears for a claw that must squeeze hard but can close slowly. Which gear does the servo turn — the smaller or the larger of the pair? Explain using the click model, not just the rule.
Phase 5 — Compound Gearing: Multiplying the Trade
A 3.75:1 ratio is good. What if you need far more? You could hunt for a giant gear — or you could stack the trick.

Put two gears of different sizes on the same axle , connected so they must turn at the same rate. Now drive the large one of the pair from one stage, and let the small one drive the next stage. Each stage keeps its own ratio — and the ratios multiply . This is compound gearing .
Stage 1
8-tooth driving 30-tooth — 30:8, or 3.75:1
Stage 2
Combined
That could be a lot of torque!
Remember — Gears Aren’t Magic

For everything we gain we give something else up. In the 14.06:1 train above, if a motor turns the gear on the far left, it must make 14 complete revolutions before the gear on the far right completes one. You bought a fourteen-fold stronger twist and paid for it with fourteen-fold slower output. The trade is exact, every time.

Build a compound train on paper from two stages, each an 8-tooth gear driving a 24-tooth gear. What is each stage’s ratio, what is the combined ratio, and how many motor revolutions does one output revolution cost?
Phase 6 — Connect: Where This Shows Up in Botball
Transfer

You now hold the language of the next dozen challenge sheets. Challenge 3 builds the pincer from Phase 1 for real. Challenge 4 changes its ratio on purpose. Challenge 5 pushes torque until it has to be measured. Challenges 9 through 14 are gears doing stranger and stranger jobs.

On a competition robot, every effector faces the same trade you learned in Phase 4. A claw wants torque and can accept slow. A launcher wants speed and can accept weak. Drive wheels want a compromise. The team that can count the trade builds the ratio it needs; the team that cannot swaps gears at random until something sort of works.
Name one job on a Botball robot where you would gear for torque, and one where you would gear for speed. For each, say what you are giving up and why that cost is acceptable there.
Phase 7 — Individual Reflection
Complete this section on your own.
1. Explain the click model in your own words, and use it to show why a small gear driving a big gear produces a slower, stronger output.
2. Two meshed gears must turn opposite ways, yet a pincer needs its jaws to close together , and some mechanisms need two parts turning the same way. Explain how gears serve both needs.
3. “Gears aren’t magic.” State the trade precisely for a 5:1 gear train — what exactly is gained, and what exactly is paid?
4. Complete this in 2–3 sentences: “When I watch any geared machine now, the first two things I will look for are...”
Extension Challenges
Finished early? Try one or more of these. Extensions C and D use parts if you have them.
Extension A — The Ratio Table
List the tooth counts of every gear size in your kit.
Build a table of every two-gear pairing and its reduced ratio.
Circle the largest single-pair ratio your kit can make. Keep this table — you will use it for the rest of the module.
Extension B — Design a Ratio on Paper
A mechanism needs its output to turn once for every 9 turns of the motor.
Using only the gear sizes from Extension A, design a train that gets as close to 9:1 as possible. Compound stages are allowed.
Show the multiplication, and state how close you got.
Extension C — Hear the Clicks
Mesh two different-sized gears from your kit and mark one tooth on each with tape.
Turn the small gear exactly five rotations. Predict first, then count, how many rotations the large gear makes.
Did the count match the tooth math exactly? If it was off, what happened?
Extension D — Gear Hunt
Find a geared machine outside robotics — a bicycle, a hand whisk, a wind-up toy, a pepper grinder.
Work out whether it gears for speed or for torque, and how you can tell.
Where is its drive gear, and where is its driven gear?

prose: Overview
In Challenge 1 you moved poms sideways. Now you have to move them up — into a container whose opening is well above your machine's head.
This challenge looks like a lifting problem. It is really a shape-changing problem, and the numbers in the constraints are where that hides. Read them carefully before you start planning.
Core Insight
A machine is not stuck at the size it starts. Arms swing, sections slide, linkages unfold. Almost every tall robot you have seen began the match short.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Find a hidden requirement by comparing two numbers in a set of constraints.
Describe at least three mechanical ways a machine can gain height after it starts.
Explain why a tall, loaded machine tips, using center of gravity .
Build and refine an effector that lifts and releases a load at height, reliably.
Phase 1 — Find the Problem
Before reading any further, look at these two numbers from the challenge and work out what they mean together.
Container opening
17 inches above the floor
Your machine at the start
must be less than 12 inches tall
Subtract. How many inches of height must your machine gain after the run begins?
The Real Problem
You are not being asked to build something 17 inches tall. You are being asked to build something under 12 inches tall that becomes tall enough. That is a different machine entirely.
A design that ignores this will pass every test on the workbench and fail the moment it is measured at the start line.
Phase 2 — Concept: Ways to Gain Height
Machines that start small and end tall use one of a handful of tricks. Here are four. Each has a cost as well as a benefit — there is no free height.
Which of the four would you try first, and what is the biggest risk in that choice?
Phase 3 — Concept: Why Tall Machines Fall Over

Every object behaves as though its entire weight is concentrated at a single point. That point is the center of gravity . For a machine sitting on the floor, one rule decides whether it stands or falls:
The Tipping Rule
If the center of gravity stays above the machine's base, it stands. If it moves out past the edge of the base, it tips.

This is why your challenge gets harder as your lift rises. Raising poms moves weight upward, and swinging an arm out moves weight sideways. Both push the center of gravity toward the edge of the base — and a machine that was perfectly stable while loading can topple at full extension.
Three Things You Can Do About It
Widen the base. The farther apart the feet, the farther the center of gravity can travel before it escapes.
Keep the weight low. Put motors and heavy parts near the floor, not up on the arm.
Counterweight. Add weight on the opposite side of the pivot to pull the center of gravity back.
Reach Costs Torque

There is a second penalty. The farther your load sits from the pivot, the harder the motor has to work to hold it — that distance is called the moment arm . Doubling the length of an arm roughly doubles the strain on whatever is driving it, with the same poms in the bucket.
You will put real numbers on this in Challenge 5. For now, just know the penalty exists, and expect a long arm to struggle where a short one did not.
Predict where your design will be least stable — at rest, mid-lift, or fully extended? Explain using the tipping rule.
Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Problem
Poms need to be placed into a container whose top is 17 inches above ground level.
The Need
Lift poms from ground level to a height of more than 17 inches and release them into the container.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
The total height of your robot and lifting system must be less than 12 inches before you start your run.
You must lift at least 4 poms and place them into the container.
Your device must consistently grab, elevate, and drop poms into the container: a success rate greater than 90%.
LEGO structure and KIPR electronics only. No other materials on this challenge.
Added Value
Your device lifts several groups of poms rather than one, or
Your device runs a continuous “supply chain” of poms into the bin.

Break the build into manageable steps.

Phase 6 — Connect: Where This Helps in Botball
Transfer
Starting-size limits are not a classroom invention. Botball games set a size box every robot must fit inside before the match begins.

That rule is why competitive robots unfold. A team that designs to the size box from the first sketch has a working machine. A team that builds a tall robot and then tries to make it shorter usually starts over.
Name a Botball task that needs height your robot would not have at the start line. Which of the four strategies from Phase 2 would you use, and why that one?
Your design had to be both short and tall. Name another pair of requirements that pull against each other in robot design, and say how you would settle the conflict.
Phase 7 — Individual Reflection
Complete this section on your own.
1. The 12-inch limit was never stated as “your machine must change shape.” How did you work that out from the numbers? What does that suggest about reading constraints carefully?
2. Explain the tipping rule in your own words, using your machine as the example.
3. Compare this challenge to Challenge 1. Which was harder, and was it harder for a different reason than you expected?
4. Complete this in 2–3 sentences: “A machine does not have to stay the size it started. This means that when I am given a size limit, I should...”
Extension Challenges
Finished early? Try one or more of these.
Extension A — Raise the Bar
Keep the same starting envelope, but deliver into a container with its top at 22 inches.
What broke first — reach, stability, or motor strength?
How much height can your strategy give you before it stops working entirely?
Extension B — Shrink the Envelope

Did you have to change strategy, or just proportions?
Which of the four approaches folds down smallest?
Extension C — Find the Tipping Point

Widen the base and repeat. Record the new number.
Add a counterweight and repeat again. Which change bought you the most, and was that what you expected?
Extension D — Supply Chain
Build the added-value version: poms feeding continuously into the bin rather than one load at a time.
Time how long 12 poms take, continuous versus one trip at a time.
At what number of poms does the continuous design finally win?

prose: Overview
Back in Challenge 1 you were asked to build a pincer with no instruction at all, and told to keep notes on what fought you. This is the challenge where that gets answered.
The problem you almost certainly hit: making both arms move, in coordination, from a single motor. One arm is easy. Two arms that mirror each other is a different problem — and the solution is gears.
Core Insight
Two meshed gears cannot move independently. Turn one and the other must turn, in the opposite direction, by an amount you can predict exactly.
That is not a limitation. It is the whole point — it is how you get coordination without a second motor.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Explain why a claw with one fixed side pushes objects sideways, and a pincer does not.
Predict the direction a meshed gear will turn.
Use an idler gear to make two arms turn the same way instead of opposite ways.
Build a stable pincer that grabs and lifts poms reliably.
Look back at your Challenge 1 notes before you start. What you wrote there is about to be useful.
Phase 1 — Observe: Two Kinds of Claw
A demo bot claw usually has one jaw fixed in place and one jaw that swings. It works, and it is simple to build. But it does something to the object that you may not want.
Why would shoving the object sideways be a problem on a game field? Name a situation where it would cost you.
Phase 2 — Concept: Meshed Gears Turn Opposite Ways
Gears have teeth. When two gears are close enough for their teeth to interlock, they mesh — and from that moment neither can move without the other.
The Direction Rule
Two meshed gears always turn in opposite directions. If one goes clockwise, the other goes counterclockwise. There is no exception.

That rule is exactly what a pincer needs. Put a gear at the base of each arm, mesh the two gears together, and drive just one of them. The other is forced to turn the opposite way — which swings the second arm inward as the first swings inward.
Answer These Before You Build

What direction does that cause the other arm to move?
Does that meet the need — do both arms close on the pom together?
Phase 3 — Concept: The Idler Gear
Sometimes you want the opposite of a pincer — two arms moving the same direction together, like a pair of sweepers or a conveyor. Two meshed gears cannot do that. But three can.
The Trick
Put a third gear between the two. It reverses the direction once, and then reverses it again — so the two outer gears end up turning the same way.
That middle gear is called an idler gear . It changes direction without changing speed at all.
You will not need an idler for this challenge — a pincer wants opposite directions. But remember it exists. It is one of the most reusable tricks in this module.
Name a robot job that would need two arms turning the same direction rather than closing on each other.
Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
Project Overview
Using your kit, design, create, and modify a pincer that is stable, can effectively grab 3 poms or more, and lift them with a success rate greater than 90%.
Needs

The pincer must be attached to a servo or motor.
The mounting system must be low enough to let the robot pick poms up from the surface, and must be easily detachable from the robot with 2 screws or nuts or fewer.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
Use no metal pieces other than screws, bolts, and nuts.
The claw needs a 5″ minimum width when open.
The claw must reach to within 1″ of the surface to grab and hold poms sitting on it.
No non-kit parts can be used.
Why This One Is Strict

This is the tightest materials rule in the whole module — kit parts only, and no metal beyond fasteners. That is deliberate. Without a metal bar to make a rigid linkage, the only way to coordinate two arms is to solve it with gears, which is the thing this challenge is teaching.

Phase 5 — Test & Iterate
Expect Slop
Meshed gears never fit perfectly. There is always a little play between the teeth, so an arm can wiggle a small amount before the gear actually catches. That play is called backlash .
Backlash is why your pincer may not close to exactly the same spot every time. Some is unavoidable. Too much means your gears are mounted too far apart, or something is flexing.

prose: Overview
Your Challenge 3 pincer grabs poms. Poms are soft, small, and round — they do not care much where the jaws touch them.

Now you have to grab a 4-inch cube. A cube has flat sides, and this challenge demands that your jaws lie along those sides rather than poking at them. Try it with your existing pincer first. It will almost certainly fail, and the way it fails is the lesson.
Core Insight
Gears do not just transmit motion — they set the exact amount of it. Change the tooth counts and you change how far each arm swings.
That is the tool you need here, because the two sides of this grabber do not have to move the same distance.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Count teeth and calculate the gear ratio between two meshed gears.
Predict how far a driven gear turns when the drive gear turns once.
Explain the trade between torque and speed.
Use tooth counts to give two arms different ranges of motion on purpose.
Phase 1 — Try It First, Then Read On
Take the pincer you built in Challenge 3 and try to grab the cube with it. Do not modify anything yet. Just try.
What happened? Where exactly did the jaws touch the cube?
Why It Fails

Arms that pivot swing through an arc. That means the jaw faces are only parallel to the cube at one exact moment of the swing — and at the point where the jaws actually make contact, they are usually tilted. A tilted jaw touches a flat face at a corner, not along its length.

There is more than one way out of this. You can add a second pivot at the jaw so it can swivel flat. You can build a linkage that keeps the jaws parallel. Or you can shorten the swing so the jaws barely rotate at all — which is where gear ratios come in.
Phase 2 — Concept: Teeth, Mesh, and Ratio
Gears, or sprockets, have a set number of teeth. For two gears to work together, their teeth must have a mesh location — a place where they interlock.

Now think about counting. A 10-tooth gear has to click through 10 teeth to make one full rotation. An 8-tooth gear only has to click through 8. So if you mesh them and turn one, they do not come out even.
Work It Out Before You Read the Answer
The gear on the left has 8 teeth. The gear on the right has 16. If you turn the left gear one full rotation clockwise, what happens to the gear on the right?
Your answer, before you look:
The Answer
If the gear on the left turns one full rotation clockwise, the gear on the right turns half a rotation counterclockwise. That is a 2:1 gear ratio.
The rule: divide the driven gear's teeth by the drive gear's teeth. 16 ÷ 8 = 2, so a 2:1 ratio. An 8-tooth driving a 30-tooth gives 30 ÷ 8 = 3.75, so 3.75:1.
Your Challenge 3 pincer used the same gear on both sides — a 1:1 ratio. What did that guarantee about how the two arms moved?
Phase 3 — Concept: What a Ratio Buys You
Gears that mesh but have different tooth counts give you an advantage. Which advantage depends on which gear you drive.
Drive the small gear
You gain torque . The output turns slower but pushes harder. Use this when something is heavy or stubborn.
Drive the large gear
You gain speed . The output turns faster but pushes with less force. Use this when something needs to move quickly.
What Torque Actually Means
A linear force is a push or a pull. A torque is a twist — the turning equivalent of a push.
When you say a gear train “has more torque,” you mean the output shaft can twist against more resistance before it stalls.
Gears Are Not Magic

Everything you gain, you give up somewhere else. A 3.75:1 ratio gives you 3.75 times the twist — and costs you 3.75 times the rotations to get there. There is no arrangement of gears that gives you more of both.
Why This Matters Here
Read the third constraint of this challenge again: both sides of the pincer must rotate, however they do not have to have the same range of motion.

That sentence is permission. You are allowed to put a different gear on one side than the other — so one arm sweeps far while the other barely moves. Used well, that is one way to keep a jaw face flat against the cube.
If you put a 16-tooth gear on one arm and an 8-tooth gear on the other, both driven by the same gear, which arm sweeps farther, and by how much?

prose: Overview

This is where the first four challenges come together. You are going to build an arm that folds under a starting height limit, unfolds to reach a bin, grabs a real object with a true pincer, and does all of it without overworking a single motor.
From Challenge 2
The 12″ starting envelope, and the tipping rule for a loaded arm.
From Challenge 3
A true pincer where both jaws move, driven by meshed gears.
From Challenge 4
Gear ratios — and this time you will use them to survive a load, not to aim a jaw.
Core Insight
Up to now you have found out whether a design works by building it and watching. This time you can know beforehand. Torque is arithmetic, and the arithmetic is not hard.
Materials Open Up Here

Challenges 3 and 4 were strictly kit parts. This one permits a few metal pieces beyond fasteners, and it permits counterweights — up to 100 pennies, or a robot controller. That is not a loophole. It is a tool you are expected to use.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Count and name the degrees of freedom in a mechanism.
Calculate the torque at a joint from weight and distance.
Reduce the torque a motor experiences using a counterweight or gear reduction .
Verify on paper that a design meets a numeric limit before building it.
Phase 1 — Concept: Degrees of Freedom
The challenge asks for “no less than 3 axis of movement.” The proper name for what it is counting is degrees of freedom , usually shortened to DOF.
The Definition
A degree of freedom is one independent way a mechanism can move. Independent means it can change without anything else having to change.
Count the joints that a motor or servo can drive separately. That is your DOF count.
Your Challenge 3 pincer had exactly one. Both arms moved — but they were geared together, so they were not independent. One motor, one motion, one degree of freedom.
A Practical Note About Your Kit

A base that spins the whole arm around a vertical axis is the fourth joint you may be imagining. It is hard to build well with the parts you have, because there is no large ring bearing to carry the arm's weight while it turns.
Shoulder, elbow, and gripper is the achievable three. If you want a fourth, add a wrist that tilts the gripper.
List the three joints you plan to build and say what each one does.
Phase 2 — Concept: Calculating Torque
In Challenge 4 you learned that torque is a twist. Now you need a number for it.
That distance from the pivot to the load is the moment arm . It matters as much as the weight does — and it is the part students forget.
Do Not Forget the Arm Itself
Your arm has weight too, and that weight also sits out at a distance. Treat the arm as though all of its weight acts at its middle — that is its center of gravity — and add its torque to the load's.
Worked Example
A 10 oz object, 12 inches out: 10 × 12 = 120 oz-in
The arm weighs 4 oz and is 12 inches long, so its weight acts 6 inches out: 4 × 6 = 24 oz-in
A counterweight of 9 oz sits 5 inches out on the other side: 9 × 5 = 45 oz-in
Total at the shoulder: 120 + 24 − 45 = 99 oz-in
A US penny weighs roughly 0.09 oz, so 100 pennies come to about 9 oz. Weigh your controller rather than guessing — they are heavier than students expect.
99 oz-in is under the 120 limit. But this arm is only 12 inches long. What happens to the number if you need 18 inches of reach instead? Work it out.
Phase 3 — Concept: Staying Under the Limit
You have a budget: no motor or servo may experience more than 120 oz-in. There are four ways to stay inside it.
Shorten the arm
Torque scales directly with distance. Half the reach is half the torque. Cheapest fix, but you still have to reach the bin.
Lighten the arm
Every ounce you remove from the far end removes several oz-in. Move motors toward the base.
Counterweight
Weight on the far side of the pivot subtracts. Up to 100 pennies or a controller is permitted here.
Gear reduction
The one that changes what the motor feels rather than what the joint feels.
How Gear Reduction Helps
The first three change the torque at the joint. Gearing down changes how much of that torque reaches the motor.
So a joint carrying 150 oz-in — over the limit — driven through a 3.75:1 reduction puts 150 ÷ 3.75 = 40 oz-in on the motor. Comfortably inside the budget.
Remember What It Costs
Gears are not magic. That same 3.75:1 reduction means the motor must turn 3.75 times for every one turn of the joint. Your arm gets strong and slow at exactly the same rate.
If One Reduction Is Not Enough
Gear pairs can be stacked, and their ratios multiply. Two 3.75:1 pairs in series give 3.75 × 3.75 = 14.06:1 — a very large reduction from a small stack of gears.
That is called compound gearing, and you will work with it properly later in the module. For now, know that the option exists if a single pair leaves you over budget.

prose: Overview
Motors turn. That is the only thing they do. Gears change how fast and how hard they turn — that was Challenges 3 through 5 — but the motion coming out is still rotation.

Most jobs a robot has to do are not turning jobs. They are pushing, lifting, sliding, and grabbing jobs. Somewhere between the motor and the task, the kind of motion has to change. That is what this new set of challenges is about, and the crank is the simplest example of it.
Core Insight
A mechanism is a translator. It takes the motion a motor can make and turns it into the motion the job actually needs.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Explain how a crank converts rotary motion into linear motion.
Predict the stroke of a crank from the position of its pin, before building it.
Identify the two dead points in a crank cycle and explain why they matter.
Modify a mechanism to meet a stated need under stated constraints.

Phase 2 — Concept: How a Crank Works

A crank has three working parts. A wheel or arm turns around a fixed center. A pin is attached to that wheel, off to one side of the center — not in the middle. A connecting rod links that pin to whatever you want to push.

Because the pin is off-center, it travels in a circle. The far end of the connecting rod cannot travel in a circle — it is held so that it can only slide back and forth. So every full turn of the wheel drives the far end forward once and back once.
The Two Motions
Rotary motion
Turning around a center point. This is what a motor produces.
Linear motion
Moving in a straight line, back and forth. This is what a pusher needs.
You Can Calculate the Stroke
How far the pin sits from the center of the wheel decides exactly how far your pusher travels. Not roughly — exactly.
The Two Dead Points

Look at the diagram again. In both of the positions drawn, the connecting rod and the crank arm are lined up in a straight row. Those two moments are called dead points , and they are where the mechanism has the least ability to push.

It matters for two reasons. A crank started from a dead point may just jam instead of turning. And the pusher does not travel at a steady speed — it is slowest at the ends of its stroke and fastest in the middle.
Predict: if you move the pin twice as far from the center of the wheel, what happens to the stroke? Give a number, not a description. You will test it in Phase 5.

Find Your Dead Points
Turn the wheel slowly until the connecting rod and the crank arm line up. That is a dead point. There are two of them, half a turn apart. Mark both on your wheel with a piece of tape or a marker.

prose: Overview
Your crank pushed and pulled, forward and back, over and over, evenly. Every part of every turn did something.

Sometimes that is wrong. Sometimes you want a motor to run continuously but the machine to act only once in a while — a nudge, then nothing, then another nudge. That is what a cam does, and the shape of the cam decides exactly when the nudge happens.
Core Insight
A crank gives you the same motion throughout every turn. A cam lets you choose which part of the turn does the work — and the rest of the turn does nothing at all.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Explain the difference between a cam and a crank.
Shape a cam profile so its raised section covers a measured portion of the turn.
Explain why every cam needs a return force .
Build a mechanism that grabs and pushes an object intermittently .
Materials Note

This challenge permits rubber bands — up to 5 on the entire apparatus. That is the first time since Challenge 5 that anything beyond kit parts is allowed, and as you will see in Phase 2, it is not a convenience. A cam needs it.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism

Phase 2 — Concept: How a Cam Works

A cam is a wheel that is not perfectly round. The part that rides against it is the follower . As the cam turns, the follower rides along its edge — so wherever the edge bulges out, the follower gets pushed.

The shape of that edge is the cam profile , and it is the whole design. A round cam does nothing at all. A cam with one bump lifts the follower once per turn. A cam with a bump covering half the wheel lifts it for half of every turn.
How to Measure the 45°

The angle is measured at the center of the cam, between the two edges of the raised section. Mark your cam like a clock face before you build it: a full turn is 360°, so 45° is one-eighth of the way around. Check it with a protractor rather than judging by eye.
A Cam Can Only Push
This is the rule that catches everyone. The cam pushes the follower out — but when the lobe rotates away, nothing pulls the follower back. The cam has no grip on it.

So every cam mechanism needs a second force to bring the follower home: gravity, a spring, or a rubber band. That is why your constraints mention it. It is not an optional extra. Without it, your mechanism works exactly once.
Which return force will you use — gravity or a rubber band? What made you choose it?
Phase 3 — Build the Bare Mechanism

Before You Go On

Check Your Angle
Measure the raised section of your cam with a protractor. It must cover 45° of the turn, within 5° either way — so anywhere from 40° to 50°.

prose: Overview
Your crank pushed in a straight line. Your cam lifted straight up. Both are useful, and both are limited — the motion goes one way and comes back the same way.

A four-bar linkage does something neither can. The end of it can swing out, dip down, come back along a different path than it went, and return to where it started. It is made of nothing but straight bars and pins, and the shape of the motion comes entirely from how long you make each bar.
Core Insight
In a linkage, the lengths are the design. Change one bar by a small amount and the whole path the mechanism traces changes with it.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Name the four links in a four-bar linkage, including the one that does not move.
Test four link lengths with arithmetic to find out whether a motor can drive them all the way around.
Explain why a linkage might rock but refuse to rotate.
Build a linkage that reaches out, grabs an object, and draws it back.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism
Watch the video below. Do not build anything yet. Watch it at least twice.
Simple mechanics 1 — LEGO four-bar linkage.
Watch For

Phase 2 — Concept: The Four Links
You almost certainly counted three moving bars. The name says four. Both are correct.
The Fourth Bar Is the One That Does Not Move
Two of the pivots are anchored to your base and never go anywhere. The distance between those two anchored pivots is itself a link — it is just built into the frame instead of being a separate piece.
That is the ground link . It counts, because if you moved those two anchor points closer together or farther apart, the whole mechanism would behave differently. Its length is part of the design.
The Names You Will Use
Ground link
The fixed distance between the two anchored pivots. Does not move.
Crank
The input link, driven by your motor. If the lengths are right, it goes all the way around.
Coupler
The link joining the crank to the rocker. It is attached to nothing fixed, which is why its motion is the most interesting.
Rocker
The output link. Usually it swings back and forth rather than spinning.
A Special Case Worth Knowing

If the crank and rocker are the same length, and the coupler and ground link are the same length, you get a parallelogram linkage . In that arrangement the coupler stays parallel to the ground link no matter where the mechanism is in its swing.
That is one of the ways to solve the tilted-jaw problem from Challenge 4 — a gripper mounted on a parallelogram stays flat all the way through its travel.
Phase 3 — Build It, Then Test the Lengths
Build the linkage out of LEGO. Do not attach a grabber yet. Get the four bars pinned together and anchored to a base first.
The Problem You Are About to Have
Attach a motor to the crank and one of two things happens. Either the crank spins all the way around, over and over — or it swings partway, hits a position it cannot get past, and stalls.
Which one you get is not luck, and it is not the motor. It is decided entirely by the four lengths, and you can check it with arithmetic before you ever turn the power on.
The Length Test
Measure all four links. Count holes, count studs, use inches — any unit works as long as you use the same one for all four. Then sort them:
Worked Example
Suppose your four links measure 2, 4, 5, and 6 holes.
Shortest is 2. Longest is 6. Added: 8
The other two are 4 and 5. Added: 9
8 is less than 9, so the test passes. Something can rotate fully.
Now suppose they measure 2, 3, 4, and 8 instead.
Shortest 2 plus longest 8 is 10
The other two, 3 and 4, add to 7
10 is greater than 7, so the test fails. Nothing will rotate fully. Every link will only rock back and forth, and a motor attached to the crank will jam.
One More Rule
Passing the test means a link can rotate. To make sure it is the one your motor is driving, put the motor on the shortest link.

prose: Overview
In Challenge 4 you worked hard for a 3.75:1 gear ratio. It took two gears of very different sizes, and it took up real space on your build.

A worm gear will give you 24:1 from two small parts. It will also turn the drive through a right angle, and it will hold whatever it is driving in place when the power goes off. Three useful things at once — and it gives up something significant in return.
Core Insight
A worm is a screw. Turn it once and it pushes the wheel along by exactly one tooth. So the number of teeth on the wheel is the ratio — no arithmetic required.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Name the two parts of a worm gear set and explain how they mesh.
Work out the ratio by counting teeth on the wheel.
Explain what self-locking means and why it matters for a robot arm.
Build a mechanism that moves slowly and at a steady rate, and prove it with a stopwatch.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism
Watch the video below. Do not build anything yet. Watch it at least twice.
Simple mechanics — LEGO worm gear.
Watch For
1. What do you notice?
2. What is happening?
3. Compare the speed of the input to the speed of the output. Which is turning faster, and by roughly how much?
What do you notice? Describe what the mechanism is doing.
Look at the two shafts. How are they pointed relative to each other? This is different from every gear pair you have built so far.
Compare this to the cam in Challenge 7 and the crank in Challenge 6. Does the output here speed up and slow down, or move at a steady rate?
Phase 2 — Concept: The Worm and the Wheel
A worm gear set has two parts. The worm is the screw — it looks like a threaded rod, and it is what your motor turns. The worm wheel is the toothed wheel that the screw drives.
People often call the whole set “a worm gear,” and sometimes call just the wheel that. When it matters, say worm for the screw and worm wheel for the wheel.
The Ratio Is the Tooth Count
The worm's thread is a single continuous spiral. Each full turn of the worm slides that spiral along by one tooth of the wheel. So the wheel advances one tooth per turn, and no more.
Compare that to Challenge 4, where an 8-tooth gear driving a 30-tooth gear gave you 3.75:1 and took up far more room.
The Drive Turns a Corner

Notice the shafts in the diagram. The worm's axis and the wheel's axis are at 90° to each other. That is not optional — it is how a worm gear has to be built. It is called a right-angle drive , and it is genuinely useful: a motor lying flat on a surface can turn something that spins about a vertical axis.
That property is what makes this challenge possible at all.
The Best Part: It Locks
Turn the worm and the wheel turns. Now try the reverse — grab the wheel and try to turn it. It will not go. The screw thread simply jams against the teeth.
This is called self-locking , and it is why worm gears show up on robot arms everywhere.

Think back to Challenge 5. Your Big Arm needed the motor working constantly just to hold a load in the air. On a worm drive it would not — cut the power and the arm stays exactly where it is, holding its position with no motor effort at all.
What You Give Up

Gears are still not magic. A 24:1 ratio means the output turns 24 times slower than the input. A worm drive is also less efficient than spur gears — a good deal of the motor's effort goes into friction between the screw and the teeth rather than into useful work.
You buy torque, holding power, and a right-angle turn. You pay in speed and in wasted energy.

Before You Go On

Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Need
Using your newly created LEGO contraption, modify and attach it in such a fashion that you can slowly rotate a marker to create a perfect circle.
Mental Picture
Your contraption will act like a protractor — one fixed center, one arm of fixed length, sweeping a smooth arc all the way around.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
The overall device must be stationary. Only the worm gear and arm mechanism can move.
The mechanism must draw a complete, closed circle.
The motor lies flat on the surface, and the marker draws on that same surface. Turning the drive through 90° is the worm gear's job — that is what makes this possible.
The marker must move at a constant speed, and one full 360° circle must take more than 60 seconds.
You may use rubber bands or tacky material to attach the marker to the arm.
Your Plan — Before You Build
How will you hold the marker so its tip stays pressed on the paper the whole way around, without dragging the arm off course?
Break the build into manageable steps.
Predict: will your first circle take more or less than 60 seconds? Say why you think so.

Time It First

Run one full circle with a stopwatch before you change anything else. The 60-second requirement is the constraint most likely to fail on your first build, because a single worm pair may not slow things down as much as you expect.

If your circle finishes too fast, you have three ways to fix it: use a worm wheel with more teeth, add another reduction between the worm wheel and the arm, or lower the motor's power setting. The first two are mechanical solutions and will hold steady. Think about which one you would trust in a competition.

An arm that stays where you put it, with the motor switched off, is worth more than an arm that is merely strong.

A motor holding a load against gravity draws current the whole time, heats up, and drifts. A worm drive holds it for free. That single property is why worm gears turn up on lift arms, on camera mounts, and on anything that has to stop at a position and stay there.

prose: Overview

This challenge does not introduce a new mechanism. It asks you to put two you already have together — the pincer from Challenge 3 and the worm gear from Challenge 9 — and it turns out the combination is better than either piece suggested.
Every gripper you have built so far needed the motor working the whole time it was holding something. Let go of the power and the grip goes with it. This one does not.
Core Insight

A worm can mesh with two gears at once — one above it, one below. Because they sit on opposite sides of the same screw, they are forced to turn in opposite directions. That is a pincer, with no second gear mesh and no idler.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Explain how one worm drives two gears in opposite directions.
Build a pincer from a worm drive rather than from meshed gears.
Test whether a grip holds after the power is cut, and say why.
Compare two ways of solving the same problem and judge which is better for a given job.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch It Again
This is the same video you watched for Challenge 9. Watch it once more, but this time with a different question in mind: the worm has two sides. What could you put on the other one?
Simple mechanics — LEGO worm gear.
Watch For
1. Where exactly does the screw touch the gear teeth?
2. If you put a second gear on the opposite side of the worm, which way would it turn?
3. Would both gears turn at the same speed?
Predict: with a second gear on the other side of the worm, would the two gears turn the same direction or opposite directions? Explain your reasoning before you read on.
Phase 2 — Concept: One Worm, Two Gears
Think about where the screw thread pushes. As the worm turns, its thread travels along the worm's length, and it shoves whatever tooth it is touching in that same direction.

A gear sitting above the worm gets pushed at its lowest tooth. A gear sitting below gets pushed at its highest tooth. Same push, opposite ends of each gear — so the two gears are forced to spin opposite ways.
Compare to Challenge 3
In Challenge 3 you got two arms moving toward each other by meshing two gears directly together. That worked, and it needed the two gears touching each other.
Here the two gears never touch. The worm alone does the whole job, and it adds an enormous reduction on the way through — which means the grip is far stronger for the same motor.
And the Grip Stays
Remember from Challenge 9: a worm drive is self-locking . The worm can turn the gears, but the gears cannot turn the worm.

Applied to a pincer, that means something genuinely useful. Close the jaws on an object, cut the power, and the object stays clamped. The gears cannot spread apart, because spreading apart would require them to back-drive the screw — and they cannot.
Your Challenge 3 pincer needed the motor holding it closed the whole time. Name one problem that causes over a long match.
Phase 3 — Build the Bare Mechanism
Mount the worm so it meshes with two gears, one on each side. Do not attach arms yet. Both gears must engage the screw firmly — a gear that only just touches will skip under load.
Before You Go On

Turn the worm by hand. Both gears should turn together, in opposite directions, smoothly. If only one turns, that gear is meshed and the other is not. If either one clicks or jumps, the spacing is wrong.
Worms push sideways as well as around. Brace the worm at both ends or it will walk out of mesh the moment there is load on it.
Test the Lock
Hold one gear and try to turn it by hand. Then turn the worm instead. Note what happens each way — you will use this in Phase 5.
Did both gears turn in opposite directions on the first try? If not, what was wrong?
What happened when you tried to turn a gear by hand?
Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Need
Using your newly created LEGO contraption, modify and attach it in such a fashion that it drives both arms of a pincer contraption.
Mental Picture
Think of a vise or a C-clamp on a workbench. You turn the screw, the jaws close on the work — and then you let go of the handle entirely and it stays clamped. The screw is what makes that possible.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
The overall device must be stationary. Only the worm gear driven pincer apparatus can move.
Both arms of the pincer must move. Neither side may be fixed.
The pincer must close on an object between 2 and 3 inches across.
Once closed, the pincer must hold that object for at least 10 seconds without slipping while you tug on it gently.
Your device must grab and hold successfully on more than 90% of attempts, counted over at least 10 tries.

Not Required — But Do It Anyway

Record what happens. If the grip holds, your worm drive is doing something none of your earlier grippers could do. If it slips, find out why — a worm that can be back-driven usually means the mesh is loose or the arms are flexing rather than the gears turning.

A robot has a limited number of motors and a limited amount of current. A gripper that holds for free gives you back both.

Once an object is clamped in a worm-driven pincer, that motor is finished with the job. It can be switched off, and on some robots it can even be reused for something else. Compare that to a gripper that must be held closed for the entire match.

prose: Overview

You have met this problem before. In Challenge 4 you had to grip a 4-inch cube with jaws that stayed flat against its faces, and pivoting arms fought you the whole way, because an arm that swings puts its jaw at an angle.

Challenge 8 gave you one way out — a parallelogram linkage, which keeps the jaw level while still swinging. This challenge gives you the other way, and it is more direct: build jaws that do not swing at all.
Core Insight
A jaw that slides in a straight line cannot tilt. There is no rotation anywhere in its motion, so there is nothing to correct for.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Explain what a rack is and how it meshes with a round gear.
Predict how far a rack travels for one turn of the pinion .
Use one pinion to drive two racks in opposite directions.
Build a grabber whose jaws stay parallel through the whole motion, and prove it by measuring.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism
Watch the video below. Do not build anything yet. Watch it at least twice.
Simple mechanics — LEGO rack and gear drive.
Watch For
1. What do you notice?
2. What is happening?
3. Compare this to the crank in Challenge 6. Both turn rotation into straight-line motion. What is different about how far each one can travel?
What do you notice? Describe what the mechanism is doing.
Your crank pushed out and pulled back the same distance every time, forever. Could this mechanism go farther if you wanted it to? What would you have to change?
Phase 2 — Concept: The Rack and the Pinion

A rack is a straight bar with gear teeth along one edge. You can think of it as a gear that has been unrolled — take a gear with a huge radius and only look at a small piece of its rim, and it is a straight toothed bar.
The round gear that drives it is called the pinion . Turn the pinion, and its teeth walk along the rack's teeth, dragging the rack sideways.
You Can Predict the Travel
Every tooth of the pinion that passes the rack drags the rack along by exactly one tooth. So a pinion with 24 teeth, turned once all the way around, moves the rack by 24 rack teeth.
How This Differs From the Crank
Your crank in Challenge 6 also turned rotation into straight-line motion, but its stroke was fixed — twice the pin offset, out and back, forever.
A rack and pinion has no fixed stroke. It keeps going as long as the rack keeps going. Want twice the travel? Use a longer rack. The pinion neither knows nor cares.
Why the Jaws Stay Parallel

A part on a rack moves in pure translation — every point on it travels the same distance in the same direction. Nothing rotates. A jaw mounted on a rack is pointed exactly the same way at the end of its travel as at the start, without you doing anything to make that happen.
Go back to your Challenge 4 notes. What exactly went wrong with the pivoting jaws on the cube, and why does translation fix it?
Phase 3 — Build It: Two Racks, One Pinion
One rack gives you one moving jaw. For this challenge both jaws must move, and they must move toward each other by the same amount at the same time.

Put the pinion between two racks, one on each side. The pinion's teeth push one rack one way and the other rack the opposite way — the same trick you used in Challenge 10, where one worm drove two gears in opposite directions.
Before You Go On

Turn the pinion by hand. Both racks should slide, in opposite directions, by the same amount. If one slides and the other does not, that rack is not properly meshed. If a rack lifts away from the pinion under load, it needs a guide holding it against the teeth.
Racks skip more easily than gears do, because only two or three teeth are in contact at a time. Support the rack along its whole length if you can.
Turn the pinion one full revolution and measure how far one rack moved. Does it match the pinion's tooth count?
Did both racks move by the same amount? How did you check?
Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Need

Using your newly created LEGO contraption, modify and attach it in such a fashion that it would be able to precisely grab an object that is about 4″ wide and 4″ tall. The grabber arms must remain parallel at all points in the motion.
Mental Picture
Think of elevator doors. Two panels, one drive, sliding apart and back together — and they stay perfectly parallel the whole way, because neither one ever turns.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
The overall device must be stationary. Only the rack and gear system and arms may move.
Both grabber arms must move, and they must stay parallel to each other at every point in the motion.
At rest, the gap between the arms must be smaller than the block. The mechanism has to open before it can go around the block, then close on it.
The device must grab a block about 4″ wide and 4″ tall.
The device must grab successfully on more than 90% of attempts, counted over at least 10 tries.
Kit parts only.
Read Constraint 3 Again
It is easy to miss what it is asking. If the jaws started wider than the block, you could just slide the whole thing over it and squeeze — the mechanism would only ever need to close.
Starting narrower forces your rack to travel both ways from its resting position: open first, then close. Make sure you have rack length in both directions before you build the jaws.

How to Prove the Jaws Are Parallel

Do not judge it by eye. Close the jaws on the block and measure the gap at the front of the jaws and again at the back . If the two measurements are the same, the jaws are parallel. If they differ, one end is pinching and the other is loose.
Then do it again with the jaws fully open. Parallel at one position is not the same as parallel at every position, and the requirement says every point in the motion.

Phase 6 — Connect: Where This Helps in Botball
Transfer
You have now solved the same gripping problem three separate ways. That is not repetition — that is a toolkit.

Challenge 4 gave you pivoting jaws, which are simple and compact but tilt. Challenge 8 gave you a parallelogram, which stays level while swinging. This gives you pure sliding, which never rotates at all. Each is right for a different situation, and knowing all three means you pick rather than guess.
Name a Botball task where sliding jaws beat pivoting ones, and one where the pivoting version would be the better choice. What decides it?

4. Complete this in 2–3 sentences: “A part that slides cannot tilt. This means that when a design keeps going out of alignment, I should...”
Extension Challenges
Finished early? Try one or more of these.

Does the rule hold every time? If a measurement is off, find out why before blaming the rule.

Grip the block again. Are the jaws still parallel? Is anything worse?

prose: Overview
The word coulisse is French for a groove or a slide. That is the whole idea: this mechanism has a pin that rides inside a slot, and the slot is cut into an arm.

Your crank in Challenge 6 was perfectly even — out and back, the same speed both ways, every turn. This one is deliberately uneven. It sweeps one direction quickly and crawls back the other way, and the motor spins at a constant rate the whole time.
Core Insight
Where you put the pivot decides how the time gets divided. Move it, and you change how much of each turn is spent going one way instead of the other.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Explain how a pin sliding in a slot converts steady rotation into an uneven swing.
Measure the quick-return ratio of your own build.
Explain why an uneven cycle is useful for striking something.
Build a mechanism that removes one object without disturbing the ones under it.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism
Watch the video below. Do not build anything yet. Watch it at least twice, and on the second viewing count along with the motion.
Simple mechanics — LEGO coulisse mechanism.
Watch For
1. What do you notice?
2. What is happening?
3. Time the arm swinging one way, then time it swinging back. Are the two the same?
What do you notice? Describe what the mechanism is doing.
Find the pin and the slot. Describe what the pin does inside the slot as the wheel goes around.
Was the swing the same speed in both directions? If not, which direction was faster?
Phase 2 — Concept: A Pin in a Slot
A wheel turns, carrying a crank pin near its edge — so far this is exactly the crank from Challenge 6. What is different is what the pin connects to.

Instead of a rod, the pin sits inside a slot cut lengthwise into a long arm. The arm is pivoted at one end, far from the wheel. As the wheel turns, the pin is forced around its circle, and it drags the arm along with it — but because the pin can also slide up and down inside the slot, the arm does not have to follow the circle. It just swings.
The result is oscillation : the arm rocks back and forth between two limits, over and over.
Where the Unevenness Comes From
The arm reaches the end of its swing at two particular moments in the wheel's turn. Those two moments cut the pin's circular path into two arcs — and the arcs are not the same size.
The wheel turns at a steady rate, so the bigger arc takes more time. The arm spends most of the turn going one direction and only a small part coming back. That is quick return .
Why That Is Worth Having
Some jobs need speed in one direction only. A strike, a stamp, a cut, a slap — the working stroke wants to be fast and forceful, and the return is dead time you would rather get over with.
Your task in this challenge is exactly that shape. You need to hit a pom hard enough to knock it clear. Coming back afterwards accomplishes nothing.
Compare this to your crank. In a crank, is there any way to make one stroke faster than the other? Explain why or why not.
Phase 3 — Build the Bare Mechanism
Build the wheel, the pin, and the slotted arm. Do not attach an effector yet. Get the arm swinging freely first.
Before You Go On
Turn the wheel by hand through five full rotations. The pin should slide smoothly along the slot without binding, and the arm should reverse cleanly at both ends.
The most common problem is a slot that is too tight or too short. If the pin jams at the far end of its travel, the slot needs to be longer.
Measure the Unevenness
Run the motor and time each stroke with a stopwatch. Because the strokes are short, time ten full cycles and divide, rather than trying to catch one.

Then find the two reversal points: turn the wheel slowly by hand and mark the pin's position at the exact moments the arm stops and changes direction. Those two marks divide the circle into your two arcs.
Which stroke was faster, and roughly by how much?
Where did you place the pivot relative to the wheel? What do you think would happen to the unevenness if you moved it closer?
Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Need
Using your newly created LEGO contraption, modify and attach it in such a fashion that it would be able to “slap” the top pom off of a stack of poms.
Mental Picture
Think of flicking the top card off a deck. One quick strike, the card is gone, and the rest of the deck has not moved at all.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
The overall device must be stationary. Only the coulisse mechanism and effector arm may move.
The arm must be between ¾″ and 2″ tall.
The base of the arm must sit between 1¼″ and 1¾″ off the ground.
Only the top pom may come off. The poms underneath must stay where they are.
The device must succeed on more than 90% of attempts, counted over at least 10 tries.
Kit parts only.
Those Two Height Numbers Are the Whole Problem

Constraints 2 and 3 look like arbitrary dimensions. They are not. Together they define a window: the arm has to pass above the bottom layer of poms and still be tall enough to catch the one sitting on top.
Too low and you plough through the base of the stack. Too high and you swing over everything and hit nothing. Get the window right and constraint 4 takes care of itself.

prose: Overview
You already know how to turn a drive through 90°. The worm gear in Challenge 9 did exactly that. So why is there a second challenge about the same problem?
Because a worm gear would be a terrible way to drive a wheel, and understanding why is the point of this challenge.
Core Insight

Two mechanisms can solve the same geometric problem and still be completely different tools. The worm buys you huge reduction and a grip that holds. Bevel gears buy you speed and efficiency. Which one you want depends on the job, not on the geometry.
This One Drives
Every challenge so far has started with “the overall device must be stationary.” This one does not. You are building a vehicle that moves under its own power, on a chassis , across the floor.
That changes how you test. A mechanism that works on the bench can still fail once the whole thing is rolling.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Explain how bevel gears differ from a worm gear, in geometry and in behavior.
Say why a wheel drive wants a back-drivable mechanism, not a self-locking one.
Build a chassis where the motor points one way and the wheels turn another.
Test a moving vehicle for repeatability rather than a bench mechanism.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism

2. What is happening?

Phase 2 — Concept: Bevel Gears, and Why Not a Worm

A bevel gear is an ordinary gear whose teeth are cut on a slanted face instead of a straight rim — the body is shaped like a cone with its point cut off. Mesh two of them and the drive turns a corner.
The teeth themselves behave exactly like spur gear teeth. They roll against each other, the tooth counts set the ratio, and very little is lost along the way.
The Geometry Is Different
Both mechanisms turn the drive 90°, but they do it differently, and the difference is easy to see once you look for it.
The Behavior Is Very Different
Worm drive
Bevel drive
Ratio from one pair
Huge — the wheel's whole tooth count, often 24:1
Ordinary — set by tooth counts, often 1:1
Speed at the output
Much slower than the motor
Can be exactly the motor's speed
Efficiency
Poor — the screw slides against the teeth and wastes energy as heat
High — the teeth roll against each other, like spur gears
Can the output drive the input?
No. It self-locks.
Yes, freely.
Best used for
Holding a position, or a big slowdown in a small space
Passing power around a corner without giving up speed
Why a Worm Would Ruin This Vehicle
Look at the row about self-locking. On a gripper that was the best feature the worm had. On a wheel it is a disaster.

A self-locking drive cannot coast. The vehicle stops dead the instant power is cut, you cannot push it by hand, and it fights every bump instead of rolling over it. Add the 24:1 slowdown and the wasted energy, and you have a vehicle that is slow, inefficient, and awkward.
Driving a wheel is the case where you want the exact opposite of everything a worm gear offers.
You Have Seen This Before

Go back to Challenge 1 and the automotive differential. The reason a car's driveshaft can run front to back while its wheels turn side to side is a pair of bevel gears inside the differential housing.
You met this mechanism on the first day of the module, before you had a name for it.

Bevel gears push each other apart along their shafts as they work — that is what the slanted teeth do. If your shafts are not held firmly at the right spacing, the gears will separate under load and skip. Brace both shafts before you put a motor on it.

Think of a rear-wheel-drive car. The engine sits at the front and its driveshaft runs the length of the car, front to back. The wheels turn on an axle that runs side to side. Somewhere under the back of the car, a pair of bevel gears makes that corner — the same corner you are about to build.
