prose: Overview

Your cam in Challenge 7 gave you motion that happened only part of the time. That was useful, but it was rough — the follower rose and fell wherever the cam profile happened to put it, and nothing held it still.

This mechanism does the same job with precision. It moves its output exactly one quarter turn, stops it dead, holds it locked in place, then moves it exactly one quarter turn again. The stops are not approximate. They are the same four positions every single cycle, forever.
About the Name

You may see this called the Maltese mechanism , because the slotted wheel is shaped like a Maltese cross. Engineers usually call it a Geneva drive , after the Geneva-made watch movements it was first used in. If you go looking for more information, search for the Geneva drive — you will find far more.
Core Insight
Most mechanisms are built to move something. This one is built to move something and then refuse to let it move until the next step is due.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Name the parts of a Geneva drive and explain how the pin and slot work together.
Explain what dwell is and why this mechanism has so much of it.
Explain how the drive locks its output between steps.
Tune a mechanism to hit a timing target by measuring and adjusting.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism
Watch the video below. Do not build anything yet. Watch it at least twice.
Simple mechanics — LEGO Maltese cross, or Geneva drive.
Watch For
1. What do you notice?
2. What is happening?
3. Count how many times the driving wheel goes around for one complete turn of the slotted wheel.
What do you notice? Describe what the mechanism is doing.
How many turns of the driver did it take for one full turn of the slotted wheel? What does that number have to do with the number of slots?
Between steps, does the slotted wheel drift or wobble at all, or does it hold completely still?
Phase 2 — Concept: How a Geneva Drive Works
There are two wheels. The driver turns continuously, carrying a drive pin near its edge. The slotted wheel — the Maltese cross — is the output, and it has slots cut inward from its rim.

Once per turn of the driver, the pin swings into one of those slots. While it is inside, it pushes the slot sideways and rotates the cross by exactly one step. Then the pin leaves the slot and the cross stops.
Four Slots Means Four Turns

Each pass of the pin advances the cross by one slot. With four slots, the cross needs four passes to come all the way around — which means the driver turns four times for every one turn of the output.
That is a 4:1 slowdown before you add any gears at all, and it comes with something gears cannot give you: exact, repeatable stopping positions.
Dwell — the Part Where Nothing Happens
The pin is only inside a slot for a small portion of the driver's turn. For the rest of it, the pin is swinging around outside the cross doing nothing at all, and the cross sits motionless.
That motionless stretch has a name: dwell . In a Geneva drive, most of every cycle is dwell.
The Part That Does the Locking

Look at the raised disc on the driver, around its center. While the pin is outside the slots, that disc rides against the curved cutouts on the edge of the cross — and its shape physically blocks the cross from turning.

This is locking , and it is the difference between this and the cam. Nudge the arm of a cam-driven mechanism and it moves. Nudge the arm here and nothing happens. It is not being held by friction or by the motor. It is held by shape.
Compare this to the cam from Challenge 7. Both give you motion that happens only part of the time. Name two things the Geneva drive does that the cam cannot.
Phase 3 — Build the Bare Mechanism
Build the driver, the pin, and the slotted cross. Do not worry about timing yet — get the indexing working first.
Before You Go On

Turn the driver by hand through eight full rotations, slowly. Watch for three things: the pin should enter each slot cleanly without catching on the slot mouth, the cross should advance exactly one slot per pass, and the cross should not creep at all between passes.

If the pin jams entering a slot, the slot mouth needs to be wider or the pin needs to sit at a different radius. If the cross drifts between passes, your locking is not working — that is normal on a first build, and it is what you fix next.
Add the Locking

Once indexing works, add something to the driver that blocks the cross between passes. A raised disc is the usual answer, but any shape that fills the gap and clears the slot mouth at the right moment will do.
Test it by trying to turn the cross by hand while the pin is outside a slot. It should refuse.

Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Need

Using your newly created LEGO contraption, modify and attach it in such a fashion that it will function as a clock, completing one full rotation every 60 seconds and having 4 distinct positions that occur at 15-second increments.
Mental Picture
Think of a clock with only four marks on its face — and a hand that does not sweep. It sits on one mark, then jumps to the next.
Constraints

The overall device must be stationary, with only the arm rotating.

Getting to 60 Seconds
Your motor spins far too fast for this. Even with the Geneva drive's own 4:1 slowdown, the arm will race around in a few seconds on your first build.

You will need a lot of reduction between the motor and the driver. Do not try to calculate it — build something, time it with a stopwatch, and then add or remove reduction until the arm comes around in 60 seconds. Getting there by measuring and adjusting is exactly how this would be done in practice.

Phase 5 — Test & Iterate
How to Tune It
Time one full rotation of the arm. If it takes 20 seconds, you need three times as much reduction. If it takes 100 seconds, you need less. Change one thing, time it again, and record both numbers.
Do not adjust motor power to fix the timing. Power settings drift as the battery drains, and a clock that runs fast when the battery is fresh is not a clock. Fix it with gears.

Sometimes the hard part is not getting something to a position. It is getting it to the same position, every time, without a sensor telling you where it is.

You have built nine mechanisms. Each one solved a problem on its own, and each one had a limit — a crank can only stroke twice its pin offset, a cam can only lift as far as its lobe, a Geneva drive only ever gives you four stops.

Real machines are rarely one mechanism. They are two or three chained together, where each one's output becomes the next one's input. That is what this challenge is about, and it is deliberately placed at the halfway mark: before you learn nine more, prove you can use the ones you have.
Core Insight
A mechanism's limit is rarely the end of the story. Feed its output into something else and the limit moves.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:

Phase 2 — Concept: Putting Mechanisms in Series
Two mechanisms are in series when the output of the first is the input of the second. The motor drives mechanism one, mechanism one drives mechanism two, and mechanism two does the actual job.
Slop Adds Up
You met backlash in Challenge 3 — the small amount of free play in any joint. One joint's worth is usually tolerable.

Chain two mechanisms and you have at least two more joints. Their slop does not cancel out. It adds, and by the far end of the machine a small looseness at the motor has become a large wobble at the output.
Trading Force for Distance
Here is the trick that will probably get you past 6 inches. Drive the short end of a lever, and the long end moves further — in exact proportion to the arm lengths.
You Have Heard This Before
In Challenge 4 the rule was that gears are not magic — everything gained is given up somewhere else. Levers obey the same rule. Three times the distance costs you two thirds of your force.
If your machine reaches 6 inches but is suddenly too weak to push anything, that is not a bug. That is the trade, and you may need to gear down at the motor to pay for it.

prose: Overview

The number three in this challenge's title is not a suggestion. It is the exact number of independent motions a flat object can make, and therefore the exact number of drives it takes to control one completely.

This is also a different kind of machine than anything you have built. Your Big Arm in Challenge 5 was a chain — the shoulder carried the elbow, which carried the gripper. Here, three separate drives all grip the same platform at once and move it together.
Core Insight
Count how many ways a thing can move. That number tells you how many drives you need — no more, and no fewer.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Name the three degrees of freedom of an object moving in a plane.
Explain why three inputs is the right number, rather than two or four.
Describe the difference between a serial and a parallel mechanism, and what each is better at.
Build a scoop that collects, lifts, and holds a load through a move.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism
Watch the video below. Do not build anything yet. Watch it at least twice.
Simple mechanics — planar motion with three inputs.
Watch For
1. What do you notice?
2. What is happening?
3. Count the drives. Then watch what happens to the platform when only one of them moves.
What do you notice? Describe what the mechanism is doing.
Are the drives stacked one on top of another, or do they all connect to the same part? Describe the arrangement.
What LEGO pieces might take the place of each of the pieces you see?
Phase 2 — Concept: Three Ways to Move
In Challenge 5 you counted degrees of freedom on an arm — one for each joint that could be driven independently. Now count them a different way: not on the machine, but on the thing being moved .
Put a flat object on a table and slide it around without lifting it. There are exactly three things you can do to it.
Why Exactly Three Drives
Each drive you add lets you command one motion. With two drives you can put the platform anywhere you like, but you cannot choose which way it faces — the angle is whatever the geometry gives you.
With three, you control position and angle. With four you have one more drive than there are motions to command, and the extra one has to fight the others.
Three is not a design preference here. It is the count.
Your scoop has to reach down, lift up, and tip its load out. Match each of those to one of the three motions above.
Phase 3 — Concept: Parallel or Serial? Then Build
There are two ways to arrange several drives, and you have already built one of them.
Serial
Parallel
Arrangement
Joints stacked in a chain, one after another
Several drives all attached to the same platform
Reach
Large — every link adds to it
Small — limited to where all the legs can reach at once
Stiffness
Floppy at the far end. Each joint carries everything past it.
Stiff. The load is shared between all the legs.
Slop
Adds up along the chain
Partly cancels — the legs hold each other in place
The area a machine can actually reach is called its workspace . That is the real trade here: parallel machines are better at everything except how far they can go.
Build the Bare Mechanism
Build the three-drive platform first, with no scoop attached. Get all three drives moving it before you worry about poms.
Before You Go On

Move each drive on its own and watch the platform. If moving one drive forces the others to move too, something is over-constrained — a joint somewhere needs to be free to slide or pivot that currently is not.
This is the most common problem with parallel machines, and it will lock up your build completely if you leave it.
Can you move each drive independently? If not, which joint did you have to free up?
Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Need
Using your newly created LEGO contraption, modify and attach it in such a fashion that it will scoop up poms and elevate them for transporting to another location.
Mental Picture

Think of a front-end loader on a construction site. The boom raises and lowers, the arm reaches in and out, and the bucket tips — three separate controls, and the operator uses all of them to get a load off the ground and carry it away.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
The scoop must collect at least 4 poms in a single pass from a flat surface.
Poms must be lifted to a minimum of 6 inches above the surface and held there.
The loaded scoop must retain all poms while the structure is moved 12 inches by hand.
Exactly 3 motors or servos, all driving the same platform.
The scoop must reach its load position without any part of the structure touching the poms first and scattering them.
The device must succeed on more than 9 of 10 attempts.
Constraint 5 Is the Hard One
Poms are light and they roll. A scoop that drops onto them from above pushes them out of the way before it can collect them, and a leg that swings through the pile scatters it.
The approach path matters as much as the scoop does. Work out where every part of your machine will be as it comes down, not just where the scoop ends up.
Your Plan — Before You Build

Describe the path the scoop takes as it approaches the poms. Where is every other part of the machine during that approach?
Break the build into manageable steps.
Predict: will you lose poms on the scoop, on the lift, or on the carry?
Phase 5 — Test & Iterate
Set the Poms Up the Same Way Every Time

Mark the spot and use the same number of poms in the same arrangement for every run. A scoop that works on a tidy pile and fails on a scattered one has not met the need — but you cannot tell the difference unless the setup is identical.

Phase 6 — Connect: Where This Helps in Botball
Transfer
Motors are the scarcest thing on a robot. Knowing the smallest number that will do a job is worth more than knowing how to add another one.

Counting degrees of freedom is how you find that number. Work out how many ways the thing you are moving actually needs to move, and that is how many drives to budget — before you build anything, and before you find out you are one motor short.
Pick a Botball task and count its degrees of freedom. How many drives does it genuinely need, and how many would you have guessed before this challenge?

4. Complete this in 2–3 sentences: “The number of drives a machine needs is the number of ways its output has to move. This means that before I add a motor, I should...”

Where is it biggest, and where does it run out? What would you change to grow it?

prose: Overview
Two pounds is 32 ounces. Go back to Challenge 5 for a moment: there, an 8 to 12 ounce object at the end of a 12-inch arm already put you at the 120 oz-in limit of a single motor.
Now you have to lift three times that weight, five inches straight up, with one motor. A plain arm will not do it. Nothing you have built so far will do it without help.
Core Insight
A motor's strength is fixed. What you can change is how far it has to turn. Make it turn much further and it can lift much more — and there is an exact exchange rate between the two.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Explain how a scissor lift raises a platform while keeping it level.
Define mechanical advantage and calculate what you need for a given load.
Explain why gearing down for force always costs speed, using work .
Diagnose why a scissor lift struggles most at the very bottom of its travel.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism
Watch the video below. Do not build anything yet. Watch it at least twice.
Simple mechanics — vertical transitioning platform.
Watch For
1. What do you notice?
2. What is happening?
3. Watch the bottom ends of the links. Do both of them stay put, or does one slide?
What do you notice? Describe what the mechanism is doing.
The platform goes straight up, but nothing in the mechanism moves straight up. Where does the motion actually come from?
What LEGO pieces might take the place of each of the pieces you see?
Phase 2 — Concept: The Scissor Lift
A scissor lift is built from pairs of links crossed in an X and pinned together at their middle. Stack several X's on top of each other and you have a lift.

At each level, one end of the pair is pinned in place and the other is a sliding end that can travel horizontally. Push the sliding ends inward and the X's stand up taller. Let them spread apart and the whole stack folds flat.
Why It Stays Level

The two links in each X are the same length and cross at their exact centers, so both sides of the platform rise by the same amount at the same time. Nothing has to be adjusted or controlled — the geometry does it.
This is the fourth way you have met of keeping something level: pivoting arms in Challenge 4, a parallelogram in Challenge 8, straight-line sliding in Challenge 11, and now symmetry.
The Bottom Is the Hard Part

When the scissor is nearly flat, the links are almost horizontal. Pushing them inward barely lifts anything at first — but it has to push against the entire weight of the load through a very shallow angle.

That means a scissor lift is hardest to start and easiest once it is already up. If your build lifts fine when you help it off the ground but stalls from fully collapsed, nothing is broken. That is the mechanism behaving normally, and it is what you have to design around.
Predict: at what point in its travel will your lift struggle most? Say why before you build it.
Phase 3 — Concept: Mechanical Advantage, Then Build
You have been using this idea since Challenge 4 without a name for it. Here is the name.
Gearing down 10:1 gives you a mechanical advantage of about 10. A lever with a long arm three times the short one gives you 3. Stack them and they multiply, exactly as gear ratios did in Challenge 5.
And Here Is What It Costs
Nothing is free, and the reason is simple enough to write in one line. Work is force multiplied by distance, and a machine cannot produce more work than you put into it.
What This Means for Your Build

To lift 2 pounds with a motor that cannot lift 2 pounds, gear it down. Gear it down 20:1 and it can push twenty times harder — and it must turn twenty times as far to raise the platform the same 5 inches.
So your lift will be slow. That is not a fault in your design. It is the price, and it is exactly the price the equation says it should be.
Build the Bare Mechanism
Build the scissor stack first, with no motor and no load. Raise and lower it by hand.
Before You Go On

Work it through its full range by hand five times. Check three things: the sliding ends actually slide freely, the platform stays level all the way up, and the whole stack does not rack sideways when you push on a corner.
Racking is the usual problem. A scissor built on one plane folds over sideways under load — real ones are built as two scissor stacks side by side, tied together.
Does your platform stay level through the whole travel? How did you check, rather than judging by eye?
Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Need
Using your newly created LEGO contraption, modify and attach it in such a fashion that it will lift 2 lbs a distance of 5 inches or more using only a single servo or motor.
Mental Picture

Think of a scissor lift on a work site — the kind that carries two people and their tools up to a ceiling. One hydraulic cylinder pushing sideways at the bottom raises the whole platform, and the deck stays flat enough to stand on the entire way up.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
The platform must have a surface area of more than 16 square inches.
The platform must be stable and very near horizontal at all times.
The lift must raise 2 lbs a distance of 5 inches or more.
Only a single servo or motor may be used.
The lift must work on more than 90% of attempts, counted over at least 10 lifts.
Kit parts only.
Do the Math First
Work out roughly what reduction you need before you build it. You will not get this exactly right, and that is fine — the point is to start close instead of guessing.

Phase 5 — Test & Iterate
How to Check “Very Near Horizontal”
Do not judge it by eye. Measure the height of the platform at its front edge and again at its back edge, at the top of the travel. If the two numbers match, it is level. Then do it again halfway up.
Record the difference. That number is what “very near horizontal” actually means for your build.
Build Up to the Full Load
Do not start at 2 lbs. Start with nothing on the platform, then add weight in steps, recording the point where the lift slows noticeably and the point where it stops entirely.
Those two numbers tell you far more than a single pass or fail at 2 lbs would.

Phase 6 — Connect: Where This Helps in Botball
Transfer
Every time you gear down for strength, you are spending time. In a timed match, that is a real cost — and sometimes the right one.

The question is never simply "can my robot lift this." It is "can it lift this fast enough to matter." Mechanical advantage tells you the first answer, and the work equation tells you the second one comes out of the same budget.

4. Complete this in 2–3 sentences: “Whatever is gained in force is given back in distance. This means that when a motor is not strong enough, I should — and I should expect...”
Extension Challenges
Finished early? Try one or more of these.

Does the product of the two stay roughly constant? Where did the difference go?
Extension C — Find the Minimum

Record that reduction — it is the least you can get away with.
Would you build a competition robot at that number, or leave margin? Defend your answer.
Extension D — Beat the Bottom

Try moving where the drive pushes, or starting the scissor at a slight angle rather than flat.
Which change helped most, and why does it help?

prose: Overview
You built a four-bar linkage back in Challenge 8. That one was about geometry — four links, four pivots, and an arithmetic test for whether the crank could go all the way around.
This is the same family of mechanism asked a different question. Not can it move , but how hard is it to move, and does that change as it goes?
Core Insight

In Challenge 17 mechanical advantage was a number you could calculate once. In a linkage it is not a number at all. It is a value that rises and falls continuously as the mechanism travels, and the same motor that lifts easily in one position will stall in another.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Identify the driving link in a crane linkage and explain what it controls.
Explain why a crane gets harder to hold as it extends, using moment arm .
Find, by measuring, where in its travel a mechanism works hardest.
Size a gear reduction for the worst position rather than the average one.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism
Watch the video below. Do not build anything yet. Watch it at least twice.
Simple mechanics — four-bar linkage crane.
Watch For
1. What do you notice?
2. What is happening?
3. Find the link that goes down to the base and drives everything else. That is the one your motor will turn.
What do you notice? Describe what the mechanism is doing.
Does the tip of the crane travel in a circle, a straight line, or some other path? Follow it all the way through.
What LEGO pieces might take the place of each of the pieces you see?
Phase 2 — Concept: The Crane Linkage
The crane is a four-bar, arranged so that one of its links carries on past a joint and becomes the boom. Turn the short link at the base and the boom swings out or draws back in.
That short link at the base is the driving link — in the video it is the blue rod. It is the one the motor turns, and every other part of the crane follows from it.
Why the Effort Changes
Go back to the torque rule from Challenge 5: torque is weight multiplied by the distance from the pivot. On a crane, that distance is not fixed. It grows every inch the boom reaches further out.
Size for the Worst Position

This is the practical consequence, and it is the reason the challenge has “physics” in its title. If you gear your motor for how the crane feels halfway through its travel, it will stall before it reaches full extension.
Work out the hardest position first, gear for that, and everything easier takes care of itself.
Where do you expect your crane to be hardest to move — fully contracted, halfway, or fully extended? Say why.
Phase 3 — Build the Bare Mechanism
Build the crane linkage with no motor and no load. Move it through its full travel by hand.
Before You Go On
Work it from fully contracted to fully extended five times. Nothing should catch, and the linkage should not reach a position it cannot get out of.
If your crane locks up at one end of the travel, check the link lengths against the test from Challenge 8 — shortest plus longest against the other two. A linkage that fails that test will jam.
Feel Where It Is Hard
Now hang the load on the tip and move the crane by hand again, slowly. Pay attention to where it takes real effort and where it moves easily.
Where did it take the most effort by hand? Did that match your Phase 2 prediction?
Measure the horizontal distance from the base pivot to the load, contracted and extended. Record both.
Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Need

Using your newly created LEGO contraption, modify it so that there is a motor — perhaps geared up or down — attached to the bottom of the blue rod of the crane. The crane arm should extend or contract with the use of just one motor.

The blue rod is the driving link: the short link running down to the base pivot, which every other part of the crane follows. If your kit's colours differ, look for that link rather than for the colour.
Mental Picture
Think of an excavator boom folding out over a trench. One cylinder near the base does all the work, and the whole arm reaches further with every inch that cylinder moves.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
The base of the crane, as well as the motor, must be stationary.
The crane arm must extend and contract using just one motor.

The crane must carry a load of at least 8 oz at its tip through the whole travel, in both directions.
The crane must complete the full travel on more than 90% of attempts, counted over at least 10 cycles.

Do not just record whether it worked. Divide the travel into three parts — near contracted, middle, near extended — and add weight in each until the crane stalls there.

Phase 6 — Connect: Where This Helps in Botball

The habit worth taking from this challenge is not about cranes. It is about testing at the worst case rather than the typical one, and sizing motors for that worst case with something left over.

prose: Overview

In Challenge 13 you turned a drive through a right angle with bevel gears. That worked because bevel gears are made for exactly that corner — the teeth are cut on cones that meet at 90°, and nothing else.
Real machines rarely get to choose 90°. A motor has to go where there is room for it, and the thing it drives has to go where the job is. The angle between them is whatever is left over.
Core Insight
Gears are made for one fixed angle. A joint is not — it bends to whatever angle you need. What you give up is that the output no longer turns at a perfectly even rate.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Explain why bevel gears cannot solve every angled-drive problem.
Describe how a universal joint carries rotation through a bend.
Measure the speed variation a single joint produces.
Explain how a second joint cancels that variation.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism
Watch the video below. Do not build anything yet. Watch it at least twice.
Simple mechanics — 45 degree gear rotation.
Watch For
1. What do you notice?
2. What is happening?
3. The two shafts are not lined up and they are not at a right angle. What sits between them, and how does it bend?
What do you notice? Describe what the mechanism is doing.
Watch the output shaft closely through several full turns. Does it turn at a steady rate, or does it seem to hurry and then hesitate?
What LEGO pieces might take the place of each of the pieces you see?
Phase 2 — Concept: Angles Between Shafts
The angle between an input shaft and an output shaft is the shaft angle . Two of them are easy, and everything else needs something different.
The Universal Joint

A universal joint is two forked ends — each one is called a yoke — connected by a cross-shaped pin in the middle. Each yoke can pivot on one arm of the cross, and because the two arms are at right angles to each other, the pair together can bend in any direction.
Turn one shaft and the cross carries the twist round to the other, whatever angle the two shafts happen to make.
Why a Single Joint Is Not Smooth
Turn the input at a perfectly steady rate and the output does not keep up evenly. It runs slightly ahead for part of the turn and slightly behind for the rest, twice every revolution.
At a small angle you would barely notice. At 45° it is obvious, and you will measure it in Phase 5.
A drive that keeps the output exactly in step with the input is called constant velocity . A single universal joint is not one. A double joint , with equal and opposite bends, very nearly is.
Compare this to the worm gear in Challenge 9 and the coulisse in Challenge 12. Which of the three gives the steadiest output, and which is deliberately the least steady?
Phase 3 — Build the Bare Mechanism
Build a drive that carries rotation from one shaft to another at roughly 45°. Do not attach a motor or a load yet — turn it by hand.
Before You Go On
Turn the input by hand through five full rotations. The output should follow all the way round without catching or locking.
Both shafts have to be supported on their own. A joint carries twist, not weight — if either shaft is only being held up by the joint, it will bind or pull apart under load.
What did you use to get round the 45° corner? Describe your solution.
Turn the input slowly and watch the output. Can you see it running ahead and then falling behind? Describe what you see.
Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Need

Using your newly created LEGO contraption, modify and attach it in such a fashion that a motor lying flat on the base drives an output shaft mounted on a surface angled roughly 45° away from it. The output must turn continuously and smoothly enough to drive an effector.
Mental Picture

Think of a socket wrench with a swivel adapter on it. The handle sits off at whatever angle your hand can reach, and the socket still turns squarely on the bolt. The bend is in the middle, and the turning goes straight through it.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
The base structure must be stationary. Only the drive train may move.
The motor must lie flat on the base. It may not be tilted to line itself up with the output.
The output shaft must be mounted at roughly 45° to the motor's shaft.
The output must turn continuously through at least 20 full revolutions without binding, slipping, or coming apart.
The drive must keep turning the output when you press a finger against it. It cannot slip free under a light load.
Kit parts only.
About the Angle
There is no tolerance on the 45° in this challenge. Get it close and move on — what is being tested is whether the drive works at an awkward angle, not whether you hit a number.
Measure what you actually built and write it down, though. You will need it when you compare your speed variation to someone else's.
Your Plan — Before You Build
How will you support both shafts so the joint only has to carry twist and not weight?
Break the build into manageable steps.
Predict: will your drive fail by binding, by pulling apart, or by slipping under load?
Phase 5 — Test & Iterate
Measure the Speed Variation
Here is how to see something that happens too fast to watch. Mark a line on the input shaft and another on the output shaft, and set both to a starting position.
Now turn the input by hand in eight equal steps of 45° each — one full revolution. After each step, measure how far the output has turned since the last step , and write it down.
If the drive were perfectly even, all eight numbers would be 45°. They will not be.
The Eight-Step Test

Step 2 — 45° to 90°
Step 3 — 90° to 135°
Add up all eight of your output figures. Do they come to 360°? Explain why they must, even though the individual steps are uneven.

Phase 6 — Connect: Where This Helps in Botball
Transfer
Where a motor can physically fit is one of the first things that limits a robot design. A drive that bends removes that limit.

With bevel gears the motor has to sit square to what it drives. With a joint it can sit anywhere there is room, at any angle, and the drive still gets where it is going. That is often the difference between a layout that fits inside the size box and one that does not.
Describe a robot layout problem that a bending drive would solve. What are you able to fit in that you could not before?
Your drive does not turn the output at a perfectly even rate. Name a Botball job where that would not matter at all, and one where it would cause real trouble.
Phase 7 — Individual Reflection

2. Describe the speed variation you measured. Was it as large as you expected?
3. Explain how a second joint cancels the unevenness of the first. Use the words equal and opposite .
4. Complete this in 2–3 sentences: “A joint bends to any angle, but does not turn evenly. This means that when I need a drive at an awkward angle, I should...”

Finished early? Try one or more of these.
Extension A — Build the Double Joint
Add a second joint with an equal and opposite bend, and an intermediate shaft between them.
Run the eight-step test again and record all eight output figures.
How much smaller is the spread than it was with one joint? Did it disappear completely?

Did the joint hold up? What failed first, the joint or something else?

Which would you use where evenness matters, and what did that choice cost you?

prose: Overview
This will look familiar. A central gear, racks on either side, two arms closing on a 4-inch cube — that is the grabber you built in Challenge 11.

The difference is in the title. Challenge 11 was about keeping the jaws parallel. This one is about length : getting the arms out past the edge of the machine, so the object does not have to be sitting inside the base to be grabbed.
Core Insight
Racks do not only move things. A rack that slides out of its housing makes the machine longer than it was — and if that housing is itself sliding, the two add up.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Explain how sliding stages add their travel together.
Measure the reach of a mechanism past its own footprint .
Predict when an extending machine will tip, using center of gravity.
Design a base that stays put while the arms are fully out and loaded.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism
Watch the video below. Do not build anything yet. Watch it at least twice.
Simple mechanics — using linear teeth to increase length.
Watch For
1. What do you notice?
2. What is happening?
3. Compare the size of the mechanism when it is closed up to how far it reaches when it is fully out.
What do you notice? Describe what the mechanism is doing.
Does the mechanism end up longer than it started? Where did the extra length come from — nothing grew, so what happened?
What LEGO pieces might take the place of each of the pieces you see?
Phase 2 — Concept: Stages Add Up
A rack sliding out of a housing has a limit: it can only travel as far as its own length before it falls out. One rack, one stage , one amount of reach.
Now put a second rack on the first, sliding along it. When both are extended, the second one starts from wherever the first one ended — so the two travels add together.
The Cost of Reaching Out
The moment your arms cross the edge of the base, the machine has an overhang — weight hanging out past the footprint, with nothing under it.

You met this rule in Challenge 2. If the center of gravity stays over the base, the machine stands. Push it past the edge and the machine tips. Extending arms move weight outward, and adding an object at the far end moves it further still.
The Failure You Should Expect
Your mechanism will probably work perfectly on the bench and then tip forward the first time you extend it fully with the cube in the jaws.
You have three tools for this, all from earlier challenges: widen the base, keep the heavy parts back over the base, or counterweight the far side. Challenge 5 was where you first used the third one.
Predict how far you will be able to reach before your machine tips. What will you do about it?
Phase 3 — Build the Bare Mechanism
Build the central gear and the racks first, with no arms attached. Get everything sliding cleanly before you add anything to it.
Before You Go On
Run the mechanism through its full travel by hand five times. Both racks should move by the same amount and neither should skip a tooth at the end of its travel.

The specific problem with extending mechanisms is that a rack hanging far out of its housing is only supported at one end. It sags, lifts off the gear, and skips. If yours does that, it needs support further along, not more force.
Measure the footprint of your base, and the furthest the arms reach when fully extended. Record both.
Did anything sag or skip at full extension? What did you add to fix it?
Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Need

Using your newly created LEGO contraption, modify it so that there is a motor attached to the central sprocket. Each lengthening piece should have an arm at 90° that would allow it to get wider or narrower to precisely grab a 4″ × 4″ × 4″ foam object.
Mental Picture

Think of a telescoping ladder. Folded up it fits in the back of a van; extended it reaches the roof. Nothing about it grew — the sections simply slid out of each other, and each one started where the last one ended.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
The base structure of the device must be stationary.
The arms must be no less than 1½″ in height and 4″ in length.
The arms must start in a position more narrow than the object to be grabbed.
The foam cube must sit entirely outside the base's footprint. The arms have to reach past the edge of the machine to get to it.
The base must not tip, slide, or lift while the arms are fully extended and holding the cube.
The device must grab the cube on more than 90% of attempts, counted over at least 10 tries.
Kit parts only.
Your Plan — Before You Build
How many extending stages will you use, and how much reach does each one give you?
How will you stop the machine tipping forward when the arms are fully out with the cube?
Break the build into manageable steps.
Predict: will your machine fail by tipping, by the racks sagging, or by not reaching far enough?
Phase 5 — Test & Iterate
Find the Tipping Point on Purpose
Do not wait for it to happen by accident. Extend the arms a little at a time with the cube held, and note the reach at which the base first starts to lift at the back.
That number is the real limit of your machine. Everything you do to fix it should be measured against moving that number further out.

Phase 6 — Connect: Where This Helps in Botball
Transfer
A robot that has to drive to everything spends the match driving. A robot that can reach does not have to move as often.
Reaching also gets you to places a robot cannot go. If a scoring zone is behind a barrier or in a spot too tight to drive into, an arm that extends is the only way in.

A robot that reaches out far will want to tip. On a robot that also drives, what makes that harder than it was on your stationary base?

2. You built a very similar grabber in Challenge 11. What was that one really about, and what is this one really about?

prose: Overview
Your scissor lift in Challenge 17 went up when the motor ran forward and came down when it ran backward. That is the obvious way to build a lift, and this challenge forbids it.
Here the motor turns one way and never stops or reverses — and the platform still has to rise and fall. That single constraint changes the whole problem.
Core Insight
You already solved this in Challenge 6. A crank turns endless rotation into back-and-forth motion, without the motor ever changing direction. An elevator is the same trick pointed upward.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Explain how a one-way motor produces two-way motion.
Describe what a coupler curve is and trace one.
Explain the difference between a parallelogram linkage and a straight-line linkage .
Choose between a level platform and a straight path, and defend the choice.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism
Watch the video below. Do not build anything yet. Watch it at least twice.
Simple mechanics — application of parallelogram concepts.
Watch For
1. What do you notice?
2. What is happening?
3. Pick one point on the moving platform and follow only that point through a whole cycle. What shape does it trace?
What do you notice? Describe what the mechanism is doing.
Does the platform stay level as it moves, or does it tilt? Does it travel straight up, or does it swing sideways as well?
What LEGO pieces might take the place of each of the pieces you see?
Phase 2 — Concept: One Way Round, Two Ways Up
A motor that only spins one direction seems like a poor way to build something that has to go up and then down again. It is not. It is how almost every engine-driven machine in the world works.
Compare to Challenge 17
Your scissor lift needed the motor to run forward, stop, and run backward. That means someone or something has to decide when to reverse — a program, a switch, or a limit.
This elevator needs none of that. Turn it on and it cycles by itself, forever, with no decisions made anywhere. Fewer decisions means fewer things that can go wrong.
Name one advantage of a lift that reverses on command, and one advantage of a lift that simply cycles. When would you want each?
Phase 3 — Concept: The Shape of the Path, Then Build

Back in Challenge 8 you may have taped a marker to the middle link of a four-bar and let it draw. The shape it drew has a name: the coupler curve — the path traced by a point on the coupler as the mechanism runs.
That curve is not usually a circle, and it is not usually a straight line. And here is the useful part: you can change its shape by changing the link lengths .
You Cannot Have Both, Easily
A parallelogram keeps the platform level, because both moving links stay parallel to each other. But the platform swings on an arc, so it drifts sideways as it rises.

Unequal links can make a point travel almost perfectly straight up — mechanisms like this are called straight-line linkages , and engineers used them long before straight rails were easy to make. The cost is that the coupler rotates, so the platform tilts.
Which one you want depends on your cargo. Decide before you build, and be ready to say why.
Build the Bare Mechanism
Build the linkage first, without the motor. Move it through its full travel by hand.
Before You Go On
Run the linkage through five complete cycles by hand. It must be able to go all the way round without jamming — check the link lengths against the test from Challenge 8 if it locks up.
This matters more here than usual. Your motor never reverses, so if the mechanism reaches a position it cannot get past, the motor will simply push against it until something breaks.
Which version did you build, and why that one?
Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Need

Using your newly created LEGO contraption, create an elevator. You may want to modify it so that the moveable parallelogram is a different quadrilateral, or align the sprockets so that the movement is in a more vertical direction.
Mental Picture
Think of the pedals on a bicycle. Your foot goes up and then down, over and over — but the crank only ever turns one way, and the rider never has to think about reversing anything.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
The elevator must have a total lift of 3″ or more.
The rise and fall must be run by a motor in a constant spin orientation. The motor may not turn clockwise and counterclockwise.
The surface of the elevator must be at least 9 square inches — a 3″ × 3″ platform, or anything larger.
The platform must carry a 4 oz load through the whole cycle without dropping it.
The elevator must complete 10 full up-and-down cycles without fault.
Kit parts only.
Constraint 2 Is the Whole Challenge
It is easy to read past. It says your motor runs and keeps running — one direction, no stopping, no reversing — and the platform still has to come back down on its own.
If you find yourself planning to switch the motor direction at the top, you have not met the constraint. The mechanism has to do it.
Your Design Decision

The vertical difference is your lift. The horizontal difference is the drift, and that is what tells you how vertical your path really is.

Every decision a robot has to make during a match is a chance for it to make the wrong one. Mechanisms that need no decisions are the most reliable things on a robot.

A lift that reverses needs to know when it has reached the top. That means a sensor, or a timer, or a limit switch — and all three can fail. A lift that just cycles needs none of them. Switch it on and it works.

prose: Overview
Rack and pinion again — the third time in this module. The technology is familiar by now. What is new is what you have to stop the platform from doing.

In Challenge 16 you counted the ways a flat object can move on a flat surface, and got three: two directions of sliding, plus rotation. A sliding platform is a mechanism built to allow exactly one of those three and forbid the other two.
Core Insight
Most of the work in a slide is not in driving it. It is in preventing everything else. A platform pushed at one point will happily twist instead of travelling, and it will jam solid when it does.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Explain how a guide removes unwanted degrees of freedom.
Recognise skew and explain why it leads to binding .
Measure whether a platform is running square rather than judging by eye.
Build a slide that carries a load smoothly through its whole range.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism
Watch the video below. Do not build anything yet. Watch it at least twice.
Simple mechanics — rack and pinion driving a slide.
Watch For
1. What do you notice?
2. What is happening?
3. The pinion pushes the platform at one point only. What stops the platform swinging around that point?
What do you notice? Describe what the mechanism is doing.
Find whatever is holding the platform straight. Describe where it is and what it touches.
What LEGO pieces might take the place of each of the pieces you see?
Phase 2 — Concept: Taking Motions Away
A platform lying on a table has three degrees of freedom — you met them in Challenge 16. It can slide two ways and it can spin.
Your rack and pinion drives one of those. It does nothing at all about the other two, so unless you take them away, the platform will use them.
Skew, and Why It Jams

When a platform twists out of square in its guides, that is called skew . A small amount is unavoidable. Too much and the platform's corners dig into the guides, friction climbs sharply, and the whole thing stops dead — that is binding .
You Already Know This Feeling
Pull one corner of a drawer and it goes crooked and sticks. Push it square and it slides. That is skew and binding, and it is the same problem you are about to build.
The fix in a drawer is the same as the fix here: guides that are long enough, far enough apart, and close-fitting enough that the platform simply cannot get very far out of square.
Where do you think your platform is most likely to bind — at the ends of its travel or in the middle? Say why.
Phase 3 — Build the Bare Mechanism
Build the platform, the guides, and the rack and pinion. Do not add a motor or a load yet — push the platform through its travel with one finger.
Before You Go On
Push the platform from the middle, then push it from one corner. If it moves smoothly when pushed in the middle and jams when pushed at a corner, your guides are too short or too close together.
Long guides, set well apart, are what stop skew. Two short guides right next to each other allow the platform to twist between them, no matter how tightly they fit.
Does the platform move smoothly when pushed at a corner? If not, what did you change?
How far apart are your guides, and how long is each one? Record both.
Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Need
Using your newly created LEGO contraption, create a sliding platform that has at least a 2″ range of motion.
Mental Picture
Think of a desk drawer. It runs on rails on both sides, and as long as it stays square it slides with one finger. Pull one corner and it wedges itself solid.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
The platform must be a solid flat structure that will accept a LEGO or screw mount.
The platform must be at least 2″ wide and 7″ long.
The platform must have a range of motion of at least 2″.

prose: Overview
The first half of this challenge you have already solved. A motor spinning one way, driving something that drops and comes back up — that is the elevator from Challenge 21 pointed at the ground.
The second half is new, and it is in the last constraint. Stop the motor with the effector down, then pick up the whole machine and move it. The object in the claw has to come along.
Core Insight
Cutting the power does not mean a mechanism stops where you left it. Something has to be holding it — and there are two very different things that could be doing the holding.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Build a cyclical effector driven by a motor that never reverses.
Test whether your drive train is back-drivable .
Tell the difference between a mechanism that locks and one that is merely stiff.
Explain which of the two your own build relies on, with evidence.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism
Watch the video below. Do not build anything yet. Watch it at least twice.

Phase 2 — Concept: What Holds It When the Power Is Off

Your effector runs a cycle: down, hold, up, round, down again. That part is Challenge 21's trick — a one-way motor turning a gear that drives a linkage, so the effector reverses without the motor ever doing so.
Two Ways to Stay Put

When you drag the machine, the cube pushes back against the claw. Something has to stop the effector from simply folding up out of the way. There are two entirely different things that could be doing it.
How to Tell Which One You Built
With the power off and the effector down, push the claw backwards by hand and watch the motor shaft.

If the motor shaft turns as the effector moves, your drive is back-drivable. Nothing is locking. Whatever holding you have is coming from friction and from how stiffly it is built — and it will let go under a big enough load.
If the effector refuses to move and the motor shaft stays still , something in your drive train is self-locking . It will hold until a part breaks.
If it gives a little and springs back when you let go, that is flex , not holding. Note how much it moved.
Before you build: which of the two do you intend to rely on, and how will you get it?
Phase 3 — Build the Bare Mechanism
Build the gear and linkage first, with no claw. Get the effector cycling up and down from a one-way drive before you add anything to the end of it.
Before You Go On

Turn the drive by hand through five complete cycles. It must get all the way round without reaching a position it cannot pass — check the link lengths against the test from Challenge 8 if it locks up.
This matters especially here. Your motor never reverses, so a mechanism that jams mid-cycle will simply be pushed against until something gives.
Run the Hand Test Now
Stop the mechanism with the effector down. Push the effector backwards by hand and watch the motor shaft. Record what happened — you will compare it to your later result.
Did the motor shaft turn when you pushed the effector? Describe exactly what you saw.
Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Need
Using your newly created LEGO contraption, create an effector that drops down and goes back up without changing the direction that the motor is spinning.
Mental Picture
Think of the bucket on a backhoe. It drops, digs in, and lifts back out — and when the operator parks it down and drives forward, the bucket drags its load along the ground with it.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
The action must be cyclical and controlled by a motor.
The motor may only spin in one direction.
The claw on the end of the effector must be capable of securing an object 1″ × 1″ × 1″.
With the motor stopped and the effector in the down position, moving the whole structure must slide the object along with it.
The cycle must repeat 10 times without the claw losing the object or the mechanism jamming.

Constraint 4 Is the One That Will Catch You Out
Everything else is about making the mechanism move. This one is about making it not move, at the moment when nothing is powering it.
A design that cycles beautifully can still fail here, because the drag load pushes the effector in exactly the direction the linkage wants to fold. Think about it before you build, not after.
Your Plan — Before You Build

The Drag Test
Park the effector down on the cube with the motor off. Now push the whole structure along a smooth surface and measure how far the cube travels before it escapes.
Do it three times. If you get three different distances, the holding is coming from friction rather than from anything locking.

Knowing that a mechanism holds is not the same as knowing why. The difference decides whether it will still hold on the day it matters.

A mechanism held by friction and stiffness works right up until something gets heavier, or the surface gets grippier, or a collision knocks it. A mechanism held by a locking drive keeps holding. Both look identical on the bench.

prose: Overview

Every mechanism you have built so far had one motor doing one job, or several motors each doing their own. This one has a single motor doing two jobs at the same time — and the two jobs need wildly different speeds.

The striker on the front has to spin fast enough to knock a pom clear. The wheels have to creep forward slowly enough that the striker gets a chance to do it. Same motor, same instant, roughly twenty times the difference.
Core Insight
A drive train does not have to be a single line from motor to output. Split it, and each branch can have completely different gearing. One motor, as many speeds as you need.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Split a drive train into two branches from a single motor.
Give each branch its own gear ratio and predict the resulting speeds.
Explain why the tip of a spinning arm moves far faster than the shaft it is on.
Build a moving vehicle whose effector works while it drives.
Phase 1 — Observe: Watch the Mechanism
Watch the video below. Do not build anything yet. Watch it at least twice.
Simple mechanics — fundamentals of a worm gear.
Watch For
1. What do you notice?
2. What is happening?
3. Follow the power from the motor. Where does it split, and what does each path drive?

Phase 2 — Concept: Splitting the Drive
A drive train is everything between the motor and the thing being driven. Up to now yours have been a single chain: motor, gears, output.
They do not have to be. Take power off the motor shaft at two points and you have two branches , and each branch can be geared however you like.
Why the Worm Belongs on the Slow Branch

You need an enormous slowdown on the wheels and none at all on the striker. A worm gear gives you roughly a 24:1 reduction from a single pair of parts — which is exactly why it goes on that branch and nowhere near the other one.
Building the same reduction from spur gears would take three or four pairs and a great deal more space.
The Striker Moves Faster Than Its Shaft

A shaft turning at, say, two turns per second does not sound fast. But the face of a striker mounted three inches out from that shaft travels the whole way around a circle nearly nineteen inches long, twice every second.
That is tip speed , and it is why a modest motor can knock a pom clear across a table. Move the face further out and it goes faster still, for free.
Your striker has to hit hard and your wheels have to crawl. Which branch needs the worm, and what would happen if you put it on the other one?
Phase 3 — Build the Bare Mechanism
Build the split first: motor, branch point, and both branches turning — with no striker face and no chassis. Confirm that both outputs turn from the one motor before you build anything onto them.
Before You Go On
Turn the motor shaft by hand. Both branches should move together, at obviously different speeds. If only one turns, the split is not actually splitting.
Watch the worm branch especially. Under load it will try to push itself out of mesh, and if it does, the wheels stop while the striker keeps spinning — which looks like a wiring fault and is not one.
Measure Both Speeds
Count how many times the striker shaft turns while the wheel axle turns once. That number is the difference between your two branches.

Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Need

Using your newly created LEGO contraption, create an effector that spins at the speed of the motor in front and rotates an effector that can knock off the top pom of a stack of poms. The worm gear will turn a drive axle at the slower speed.
Mental Picture
Think of a propeller plane taxiing. The propeller is a blur while the plane rolls forward at walking pace — one engine, two completely different speeds, at the same time.

That 1¼″ Is Not Arbitrary
You met this in Challenge 12. The height sets a window: low enough for the face to catch the pom on top of the stack, high enough to sweep over the poms holding it up.
The difference this time is that the whole machine is moving while it happens. The face passes through that window once per revolution, and the car is somewhere slightly different each time.

Phase 6 — Connect: Where This Helps in Botball

Motors are the thing you run out of first. A drive train that splits turns one motor into two, at whatever speeds you need.

prose: Overview

Challenge 2 taught you what gears do. There is one practical problem standing between that knowledge and Challenge 3: LEGO gears do not directly match up to KIPR motors and servos. The center of a LEGO gear is a cross-shaped axle hole. The output shaft of a servo or motor is nothing like a LEGO axle. Push them together and nothing connects.

The bridge is a part you will use hundreds of times in this program: the black plastic servo horn . The horn fits the shaft; the gear screws to the horn. This PreLab walks you through that mounting step by step — and teaches the one idea that separates a mounting that works from one that wobbles, binds, and strips.
Core Insight

The gear does not just need to be attached . It needs to be attached with its center exactly on the axis it spins around. Off by a millimeter, and the gear is a different size on every side of its rotation.
By the end of this PreLab you will be able to:
Explain why LEGO gears cannot mount directly to a servo or motor shaft.
Define concentricity and explain what goes wrong when a gear is mounted eccentric .
Mount a 24- or 40-tooth gear to a servo horn with four screws, centered, in a cross pattern.
Run a spin test and read what a wobble is telling you.
Phase 1 — Observe: Two Parts That Do Not Match
Hold a LEGO gear in one hand and look at a servo or motor shaft next to it. Look closely at both centers.
The gear’s center is a cross-shaped hole , made for a LEGO axle.
The shaft is a short splined cylinder — ringed with fine ridges, made to grip a servo horn pressed onto it.

Neither was designed with the other in mind. The horn was: its center is splined to match the shaft, it comes with a center screw to lock it on, and its body is soft black plastic — soft on purpose, as you are about to use.
In your own words: why can’t the gear go straight onto the shaft, and what two jobs does the horn do at once?
Phase 2 — Concept: Concentricity

Two circles are concentric when they share the same center. For your mounting, three things must all share one center: the gear, the horn, and the shaft’s axis of rotation — the invisible line the shaft spins around.

Mount the gear even slightly off that center and it is eccentric . The gear is still round — but it no longer spins around its own middle. One side of the gear now sweeps a wider circle than the other, once every revolution.
Now remember the mesh from Challenge 2. Two meshed gears are spaced so their teeth interlock properly. An eccentric gear breaks that spacing once per turn:
On the far side of its wobble, the teeth pull away from the mesh — they skip or barely touch.
On the near side , the teeth jam into the mesh — the train binds tight.
What Eccentricity Sounds and Feels Like

A rhythmic click or grind, once per revolution. A tight spot you can feel when turning by hand. A servo that stalls or chatters at the same point every turn. Teeth that strip in one place on the gear. If a mechanism does any of these on a steady beat, check the mounting before you blame anything else.
A gear mounted 1 mm off-center is only wrong by 1 mm — yet the mechanism binds. Using the two bullet points above, explain why such a small error causes so much trouble.
Phase 3 — The Build: Gear to Horn to Shaft
Follow the steps in order. The order is doing real work — it is what keeps the gear centered.

Pick the gear and the horn. Use a 24-tooth or 40-tooth LEGO gear — both have holes around the center that screws can pass through. Use either horn: round or cross . Hold the horn against the gear and pick the one whose body sits behind the gear’s holes best.

Center the horn on the gear. Line up the horn’s center hole with the gear’s cross axle hole and sight straight through both. Look from directly above — viewing at an angle will fool you. This is the step where concentricity is won or lost.

Drive the four screws in a cross pattern. Push the 4 small servo screws through the gear’s holes and drive them into the black plastic of the horn — there are no threaded holes waiting for them; the screws dig their own threads into the soft plastic. Start all four loosely first. Then snug them in a cross pattern — one, then the one across from it, then the third, then across again — a little at a time, checking center as you go.
Mount the horn on the shaft. Press the finished gear-and-horn onto the servo or motor shaft and drive the center screw in to lock it. The technique is identical for a motor.

Spin test. Rotate the shaft slowly — command the servo through its range, or turn the motor gently by hand. Fix your eye on one point of the gear’s rim against something stationary behind it. A concentric gear holds its distance. An eccentric one visibly breathes in and out, once per revolution.
Why a Cross Pattern, and Why Only Snug

Tighten one screw fully first and it drags the gear toward its own corner — perfectly tight, and perfectly off-center. Alternating across the circle pulls the gear down evenly, the way lug nuts go onto a car wheel. And stop at snug: these screws hold by biting into plastic, and plastic that is crushed or stripped never grips again.
Which gear and which horn did you use, and why did that pairing line up best?
Describe your first spin test honestly. Clean circle, or breathing rim? If it wobbled, what did you loosen and re-center?
Phase 4 — Test: Prove the Mounting
A mounting is not done when the screws are in. It is done when it passes two tests.
Test 1 — The Spin Test
Observation
Your Result

Test 2 — The Mesh Test

If your mesh test caught a tight spot the spin test missed — or the other way around — what does each test measure that the other does not?
Phase 5 — Connect: Where This Shows Up in Botball
Transfer
Challenge 3’s pincer is driven through exactly the mounting you just made. So is nearly every powered mechanism in the rest of this module, and most of the ones on a competition robot.

Competition adds one more enemy: vibration. A robot that drives, bumps, and lifts all match long will slowly work screws loose — and screws that bite into plastic loosen quietly. Good teams put the spin test in their pre-match routine, because a mounting that was concentric last week is a claim, not a fact.
Your robot’s claw starts clicking once per revolution during a practice run. Walk through what you would check, in order, and why in that order.
Phase 6 — Individual Reflection
Complete this section on your own.
1. Define concentricity in your own words, without using the word “center.”
2. Explain why the screws go in a cross pattern, a little at a time — and what would likely happen if you fully tightened them one by one around the circle instead.
3. The horn is soft plastic and the screws cut their own threads into it. What does that make easy, and what risk does it create?
4. Complete this in 2–3 sentences: “Attached is not the same as mounted. Before I power any gear from now on, I will...”
Extension Challenges
Finished early? Try one or more of these.
Extension A — Break It on Purpose
Remount your gear deliberately off-center by a small amount.

You now know what eccentricity looks like from experience. Why is breaking something on purpose a legitimate engineering technique?
Extension B — The Other Gear

Which was easier to center, and why? Which would you rather diagnose a wobble on?

Extension C — Why Four Screws?
Thought experiment: mount the gear with only one screw, dead center of one hole. It is attached. What happens when the servo applies torque?
Now two screws, opposite each other. Better? What load does each screw carry?

Extension D — Concentricity Hunt
Find two machines outside robotics that depend on concentric mounting — a car wheel on its lug pattern, a bicycle sprocket, a fan blade, a drill bit in a chuck.
For each: how does its design force the part onto center? What is its version of the cross pattern?

prose: Overview

Every numbered challenge in this module hands you a mechanism and shows you how it works. This project hands you a task and nothing else. There is no build to copy and no mechanism named in the constraints — choosing the mechanism is the work.

That is what makes this an open design project, and it is why it lives at the end of the module rather than the beginning. The process comes from Challenge 1. The parts language comes from Challenge 2. The mechanisms come from everything since. Here you put them in service of a job.
Core Insight
Engineers do not start by building. They start by defining. On an open problem, the definition — the problem, the need, the constraints — is the only ground you have to stand on.
By the end of this project you will be able to:
Run the full five-step design process on an open problem, unprompted.
Design, build, and refine an effector that performs a sorting task.
Prove your design works with a measured success rate, not an impression.
Phase 1 — The Problem
Now you run the process with no instructions. Everything from here is yours.
The Problem
A pile of 4 poms will be in a set location. Within this stack, the bottom 3 are all the same color, and the top one is a different color.
Read This Carefully

Your machine does not need to see color. The odd pom is always the one on top, and it is always in the same place. That means this is a position problem, not a sensing problem — you already know where the different pom is before the run starts.
The Need
Perform a mechanical sort on the poms so that one color ends up on the left and the other color ends up on the right.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
You may use only 2 motors, servos, or micro servos — total.
Your device must separate the poms consistently: a success rate greater than 90%.
LEGO structure and KIPR electronics only. No other materials on this challenge.
Added Value
Your “claw” is a pincer — a grabber where both sides move, not just one.
You use fewer than 35 LEGO pieces.
About That Pincer

You own this one now. Challenge 2 gave you the gear language, and Challenge 3 taught the arrangement that makes a pincer work properly. This added value asks you to put that knowledge in service of a task — which is a different skill from building it on a worksheet.
Phase 2 — Your Plan: Run the Process on Paper
Run the five steps of the engineering design process on paper first. Do not pick up parts yet.
In your own words, what is the problem you are solving?
What must your device do? Write the need as one sentence.
List the constraints in your own words. Mark each one as a minimum, a maximum, or an approximation.
Break the build into manageable steps. What will you make first, second, third?
Predict: which step do you think will give you the most trouble, and why?
Phase 3 — Build, Test & Iterate
Reminder — Measure, Don’t Guess
You learned this in Challenge 1: a success rate is a count, not an impression. To beat 90%, you need at least 10 successes out of 10, or 19 out of 20. Run it, count it, write it down.

Check Against the Constraints
Check a box only after you have actually observed it — not because you think it should be true.
Describe one specific thing that failed. What was the symptom? What was the cause? How did you fix it?

You just ran step 5 of the design process and looped back — that loop is iteration doing its job. What did you change on the second pass, and which earlier step did the change actually come from — the problem, the need, or the constraints?
Phase 4 — Connect: Where This Helps in Botball
Transfer
Sorting is not a made-up classroom task. Nearly every Botball game asks a robot to tell one thing from another and put them in different places.

Your machine solved the problem without sensing anything, using position alone. That is worth noticing: knowing where something will be is often cheaper and far more reliable than building a machine that can figure out what it is.
Name a Botball task where your robot needs to separate one kind of object from another. Could position alone solve it, or would the robot genuinely need to sense something? Explain.
Your constraint was 2 motors. If you had been given 4, would your design have been better — or just bigger? What does that suggest about why engineers set constraints on purpose?
Phase 5 — Individual Reflection
Complete this section on your own.
1. List the five steps of the engineering design process from memory. Then say which one you spent the most time on today.
2. Explain the difference between a need and a constraint using your own device as the example.
3. Challenge 3 taught you the pincer arrangement on a worksheet. Using it here, in service of a task, was different. What changed when the pincer had a job to do?
4. Complete this in 2–3 sentences: “A design that solves the wrong problem beautifully is still a failure. This means that before I build anything, I should...”
Extension Challenges
Finished early? Try one or more of these.
Extension A — One Motor
Rebuild your sorter using only one motor or servo instead of two.
What did you have to give up? Did the success rate change?
Tighter constraints often force better designs. Did that happen here, or not?
Extension B — Piece Golf
Count your pieces. Now rebuild the same function using as few as you can.
Record your lowest working count.
Why would a real engineering team care about part count, beyond cost?
Extension C — Break the Assumption
Your design assumes the odd pom is on top. What if it were on the bottom?
Test it. Does your device still work, or does it fail completely?
A design that only works under one exact setup is called brittle . How would you make yours less brittle?
Extension D — Write the Challenge
Invent a new sorting problem for a classmate. Write it as a Problem, a Need, and three Constraints.
Trade with someone and build each other's challenge.
What was hard about writing constraints that were demanding but still possible?

prose: Overview
In Design Project A you moved poms sideways. Now you have to move them up — into a container whose opening is well above your machine's head.

This is an open design project: a task, a set of constraints, and no build to copy. It looks like a lifting problem. It is really a shape-changing problem, and the numbers in the constraints are where that hides. Read them carefully before you start planning.
Core Insight
A machine is not stuck at the size it starts. Arms swing, sections slide, linkages unfold. Almost every tall robot you have seen began the match short.
By the end of this challenge you will be able to:
Find a hidden requirement by comparing two numbers in a set of constraints.
Describe at least three mechanical ways a machine can gain height after it starts.
Explain why a tall, loaded machine tips, using center of gravity .
Build and refine an effector that lifts and releases a load at height, reliably.
Phase 1 — Find the Problem
Before reading any further, look at these two numbers from the challenge and work out what they mean together.
Container opening
17 inches above the floor
Your machine at the start
must be less than 12 inches tall
Subtract. How many inches of height must your machine gain after the run begins?
The Real Problem
You are not being asked to build something 17 inches tall. You are being asked to build something under 12 inches tall that becomes tall enough. That is a different machine entirely.
A design that ignores this will pass every test on the workbench and fail the moment it is measured at the start line.
Phase 2 — Concept: Ways to Gain Height
Machines that start small and end tall use one of a handful of tricks. Here are four. Each has a cost as well as a benefit — there is no free height.
Which of the four would you try first, and what is the biggest risk in that choice?
Phase 3 — Concept: Why Tall Machines Fall Over

Every object behaves as though its entire weight is concentrated at a single point. That point is the center of gravity . For a machine sitting on the floor, one rule decides whether it stands or falls:
The Tipping Rule
If the center of gravity stays above the machine's base, it stands. If it moves out past the edge of the base, it tips.

This is why your challenge gets harder as your lift rises. Raising poms moves weight upward, and swinging an arm out moves weight sideways. Both push the center of gravity toward the edge of the base — and a machine that was perfectly stable while loading can topple at full extension.
Three Things You Can Do About It
Widen the base. The farther apart the feet, the farther the center of gravity can travel before it escapes.
Keep the weight low. Put motors and heavy parts near the floor, not up on the arm.
Counterweight. Add weight on the opposite side of the pivot to pull the center of gravity back.
Reach Costs Torque

There is a second penalty. The farther your load sits from the pivot, the harder the motor has to work to hold it — that distance is called the moment arm . Doubling the length of an arm roughly doubles the strain on whatever is driving it, with the same poms in the bucket.
You put real numbers on this in Challenge 5 — the 120 oz-in ceiling. Expect a long arm to struggle where a short one did not, and now you can calculate why.
Predict where your design will be least stable — at rest, mid-lift, or fully extended? Explain using the tipping rule.
Phase 4 — Engineering to Meet a Need
The Problem
Poms need to be placed into a container whose top is 17 inches above ground level.
The Need
Lift poms from ground level to a height of more than 17 inches and release them into the container.
Constraints
Every one of these must be true for your design to count as finished.
The total height of your robot and lifting system must be less than 12 inches before you start your run.
You must lift at least 4 poms and place them into the container.
Your device must consistently grab, elevate, and drop poms into the container: a success rate greater than 90%.
LEGO structure and KIPR electronics only. No other materials on this challenge.
Added Value
Your device lifts several groups of poms rather than one, or
Your device runs a continuous “supply chain” of poms into the bin.
Your Plan — Before You Build
Run the five steps from Challenge 1 on paper first. Do not pick up parts yet.
State the problem in your own words. Include the height gain you calculated in Phase 1.
Write the need as one testable sentence.
List each constraint in your own words. Mark each as a minimum, a maximum, or an approximation.
Which height strategy from Phase 2 are you using, and how will the poms be released at the top?
Break the build into manageable steps.

Phase 6 — Connect: Where This Helps in Botball
Transfer
Starting-size limits are not a classroom invention. Botball games set a size box every robot must fit inside before the match begins.

That rule is why competitive robots unfold. A team that designs to the size box from the first sketch has a working machine. A team that builds a tall robot and then tries to make it shorter usually starts over.

Phase 7 — Individual Reflection

2. Explain the tipping rule in your own words, using your machine as the example.
3. Compare this project to Design Project A. Which was harder, and was it harder for a different reason than you expected?
4. Complete this in 2–3 sentences: “A machine does not have to stay the size it started. This means that when I am given a size limit, I should...”
Extension Challenges
Finished early? Try one or more of these.
Extension A — Raise the Bar

What broke first — reach, stability, or motor strength?
How much height can your strategy give you before it stops working entirely?
Extension B — Shrink the Envelope

Extension C — Find the Tipping Point

Widen the base and repeat. Record the new number.

Time how long 12 poms take, continuous versus one trip at a time.
At what number of poms does the continuous design finally win?
